I asked the lion. Minister of Agriculture a question as to the names of the newspapers to which a copy of these circulars marked ' confidential ' was sent. May I ask if or an answer to that question?
I have inquired, and I find that it was sent to all tile French newspapers, and to the Montreal Herald; and it was published in the Montreal Gazette.

Speaking for myself, I have no objection to every reasonable effort being put forward by the gentleman charged with the duty of taking the census to make it as efficient as possible. And I have nothing particular to say with regard to the issue of these circulars by Mr. C5t6 except this-that it is open to the gravest suspicion, to say the least of it, that circulars of that kind should be sent out to the French Canadian ministers of this country while no similar -circulars were sent to the ministers of any other race or denomination. I am quite willing that every reasonable effort should be put forth to ascertain accurately the number of persons of French origin or descent. I am quite willing that every such person who is fairly and justly entitled to be counted should be counted. But I do most emphatically protest against the course that has been followed in this particular regard. If a special effort were made by the deputy census commissioner to secure the largest possible return of those of his own faith and race for the census of 1901, it was pre-eminently the duty of the census commissioner and every other official in any position of importance connected with the taking of this census, to see to it that as strenuous an effort was put forth on their part to have as large a return as possible of people who are English-speaking, and who are not of French Canadian origin, who are at present residing in the Dominion or are temporarily absent. That is all I have to say-the transaction from beginning to end is open to the gravest suspicion. And I am sorry to say that, while I have tried to listen attentively to what the Minister of Agriculture said, he lias not thrown as much light on the subject as we had a right to expect; and I cannot say that his explanation is as satisfactory as it ought to have been.

Mr. Chairman, there is no desire on the part of any person who is at all worthy of the name of Canadian that we should have in the census anything but the truth and the whole truth. We want an accurate, exact statement of the population. French, English, Scotch-whatever may be their origin. I belong to a race which is in the minority in this country, the French race, which, from the fact that they were ceded to England in the eighteenth century have lived isolated for a long Mr. TARTE.
time, and which only within from forty to sixty years-since the union of the two Canadas-has come to share the national life of Canada. WThen the census was first introduced amongst the French Canadians, it was looked upon toy -them with some suspicion. I believe that they have improved in that way and have become to understand that the census meant no harm to anybody, but was designed merely for the collection of accurate information. However, I must say that, perhaps, the prejudices that at one time existed have not been altogether removed. If there is one class of the population who have done their best to remove those prejudices and to have the census fairly and accurately taken, it is the parish priests of the province of Quebec-the cur6s. And, when it was determined to have these circulars issued to the curfis, I think a wise step was taken. There is no class that has such accurate information as they have. I may say that, perhaps, there is no class of the community who live so closely in touch with their fellow-countrymen as the parish priests of the province of Quebec, and, for that matter all the parish priests of the Roman Catholic persuasion belonging to the French race. It is one of the national habits that once a year, in the month of January, the parish priests and the three wardens who compose the board charged with the temporal affairs of the parish, visit the parishioners- visit every house, not omitting any, and take a census. They have accurate information as to the condition of the population, as to who are away, who have come back, who have left for good-left forever, I should say, not for good, that would be a strange misnomer-and who have left with the intention of returning. When Mr. C0t6 issued the circular to the parish priests, he issued it to the men who were in the best position to give information. I share the view of the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte), that it probably would have been better-not probably, but certainly-if the circular had been signed by Mr. Blue instead of by Mr. C6t6, because it would have removed altogether the appearance of making it sectional. But it was not done in that way ; Mr. C0t6 signed it. He is an officer of the census department, and probably, as he was writing a French circular, the census commissioner left it to him to prepare it and sign it. That is what has taken place. My hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) will agree with me that, perhaps, there was not the same necessity for such a circular amongst the English-speaking population, the census enumerator being more likely to get from them all the information it was desired to collect. But I would deprecate any intention of making this serve any purpose except that we should have an accurate count of the population as it is.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: What was the object of having the circular marked ' confidential?'
I do not see the object.
It was a foolish thing to do.

I agree, for the most part, with what the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has said. But I do think we ought to know whether or not the chief commissioner was aware that this circular, as well as another which provoked some discussion some time ago, wei-e marked ' confidential.'

I may say in explanation of that matter, that this circular was marked confidential when Mr. Cote originally wrote it. It was sent to the Printing Bureau, and after the proofreading, the word ' confidential ' was stricken out, but, when the proof was sent back to the Bureau, it was printed without striking that word out. That is the absolute fact of the matter.
I presume that proof can be obtained ?
No doubt it can.

I do not desire to throw any doubt upon that statement, but the proofs are kept in the Printing Bureau, and I would ask the minister if he will not have that proof brought up and laid on the Table of the House.
The circular was printed in Le Temps office, and not in the Printing Bureau.

One of the most unfortunate things about the transaction is, that information which it was quite proper to procure, and which, indeed, it is desirable to procure, has been procured or attempted to be procured in 'such a way as to create certain suspicions in the minds of the people. That is the criticism which I will have to prononce upon it. I agree entirely with the right hon. gentleman, that it is not only proper but most desirable that information, not only with regard to all French Canadians, but all English Canadians in Canada, should be obtained ; and if there is any one temporarily in the United States within the conditions of the census, we should know about him. But, suppose, for example, that these circulars had been sent out marked * confidential ' only to the English-speaking portion of the population, my right hon. friend will see that it probably would have provoked criticism from certain quarters in his own province, and it would have been improper.
Yes.

I am not suggesting for a moment that any improper
motive has influenced his conduct, but it is unfortunate that the Minister of Agriculture and his officers should have attempted to obtain information in this way. In regard to some other matters upon which stress seems to be laid by the department, I think they are matters of not much importance, for instance, with reference to the circular sent out asking for the origin of the people of this country. I do not attach much importance to that myself, and certainly it becomes a very nonsensical matter to talk about the origin of people such as those in my own province who are called Martin, or Blanchard, or Payzant, because 100 or 150 years ago one of their ancestors was a Frenchman, and that they are to be entered, according to my understanding of the census instructions, as all of French origin : whereas, the Frasers and the Macdonalds in the province of Quebec, people whose ancestors have been French-speaking for a hundred years, are apparently to be considered as of Scotch origin, because 100 or 150 years ago, their ancestors married Into French families. Ever since then, it is quite possible that the inter-marriages have altogether been among French families, so what is the use of describing a person of that kind as of Scotch or English origin ? And what is the use of describing the Martins, the Blanchards, and the Payzants in my own province as of French origin ? It is of no great importance in this country. I think we are all content to be Canadians, and it is not of any importance that we should look back and say that our ancestors were English or French or Irish or Scotch. It only tends to keep alive ideas which really have no useful place in the life of this country.
Now, with respect to the cur6s in the province of Quebec, no one can make the slightest criticism upon them for taking action upon this circular, and no one, I am sure, thinks for a moment of making the slightest criticism on the archbishop or any bishop who has acted upon it. I would like, however, to point out to the Minister of Agriculture, that he seems to have overlooked one thing. He has stated that the French Canadian population is more or less of a migratory character. I do not know much about that, except what the hon. gentleman said with regard to it. But, something of the same kind is prevailing in the province of Nova Scotia. We have people in the province of Nova Scotia who go to the United States every year, engage in the fishing industry, remain therq some months and come back. There are people in that province who go to the United States and work in factories, and afterwards come back ; there are people who go to the United States and engage in domestic service for a portion of the year. Now, it would have been proper, I think, for the Minister of Agriculture, in seeking the information which is very properly sought in regard to

the French-speaking population of this country, to have also sought the same information with regard to the English-speaking population, even if the facts would not justify it to so great an extent. If he had taken that course there would not have been the slightest ground for any criticism at all, and that, perhaps, is of more importance than anything else connected with this subject, which has been discussed in the House and in the press. It is not desirable to have suggestions made such as have been made in the press, and to have such impressions produced upon the minds of the people ; it is not desirable that anything should be done, even with the utmost good faith, which would lead to any impression of that kind.
Hear, hear.
May I ask the Minister of Agriculture if the chief commissioner helped in the preparation of the two circulars that are referred to ?
I think I can say positively, No.
Did the chief commissioner see every circular before it was sent out ?
He said he saw one.
Which one was that ?
The general circular, not the one to the priests.
Was that one marked * confidential ' ?
It was. They were both marked ' confidential.'
Were both these circulars, marked ' confidential,' printed in Le Temps office ?
Yes.

Now, we have a large and thoroughly-equipped Bureau for doing the printing of the public departments, where large numbers of men are employed, thoroughly competent to do the typesetting and the presswork, just such jobs as these confidential circulars. Now, why could not that circular have been printed in the Bureau ? Was it because ' confidential ' was marked on both of them that they had to be sent to Le Temps office 1
No.

What is the explanation ? Were all these forms printed outside of the Bureau or printed in tht Bureau ? What part of the printing in connection with the census was done in the Bureau-where it all ought to have been done-and what part was done outside of the Bureau ?

The hon. gentleman may not be aware of the fact that at the present time the Printing Bureau is congested with work, and as a result of that congestion nearly all the printing of the census work has been done outside the Bureau.
In what office ?

It has been done in various offices, as it was sent out by the Printing Bureau. As a matter of fact, the schedules of the census are all marked ' confidential,' and a number of other documents in connection with the census are marked ' confidential.' But, I have explained already the reason why the word ' confidential ' appeared upon them, and I need not go over that again. The work was not sent to Le Temps office because it was marked ' confidential,' or for any other reason except that the Printing Bureau was not able to do it with sufficient expedition.
But, I understand there were other documents used in connection with the census which were marked ' confidential,' in addition to these two circulars.

They were all marked ' confidential ' when they were sent to the printers, as is usual when documents are sent to the printers, so that the information contained in them should not be made public until they were finally proof-read. This circular was marked ' confidential ' in the same way.
Then, do I understand there were no documents that were printed and executed by the census department marked ' confidential ' except those two circulars ?

No.
Mi-. CLARKE. The hon. minister gave us to understand a few minutes ago that there were other documents in connection with the taking of this census that were marked ' confidential.'
They were sent to the printer marked ' confidential,' but not so marked when they were finally issued.
Probably on the back of the envelope containing the copy they were marked ' confidential.'
I think it was at the head of the document.

According to the remarks which the hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has made, 75,000 French Canadians were overlooked in taking the census of 1801. It is a well-known fact that this hon. gentleman's name was prominently mentioned three or four months ago in respect to the census of the province of Quebec, and I wish to draw the attention of the

government to schedule No. 1 as prepared by the department. It asks for the following information : Country or place of birth, racial or tribal origin, nationality or religion. Well, now, you will notice that if a man is a French Canadian this schedule would call for that information, and if correctly given, it would be noted under this head. There can be no objection to this, but what we are taking objection to is that the deputy commissioner should send out a circular without the knowledge of the department. We believe that if, as the hon. Minister of Public Works says, a certain number of French Canadians were overlooked in 1891 and are liable to be overlooked in 1901, it would have been a proper course for the commissioner of the census to send a circular to each commissioner who would in turn supply each enumerator with a circular something on this line : You will be careful to see that schedule No. 1, asking for the origin or nationality of the various people that you are to take note of, is properly filled out. That would have covered the point far better than this circular issued by Mr. C0t6 and marked ' confidential.' We object to that, not because we have any feeling against our French Canadian friends, but we hold that this is establishing a bad precedent and that it is not a step in the right direction. What we are trying to do Is to have both races live agreeably together in this country. When the hon. Minister of Public Works charges that we are raising something of a racial cry, I deny that statement. The hon. gentleman was in my constituency previous to the election and I may say that he was; received well and treated well. We have heard a great deal about the hon. gentleman himself in respect to racial cries. Some of us believe that the hon. gentleman is inclined to do a little of that kind of tiling himself. I have never raised the racial cry. My father was born in the city of Quebec, and I have a warm feeling towards Quebec, though I am not a French Canadian. I have no desire to raise such a cry and no sympathy with any person who does so.

The two circulars sent by Mr. CotS have been read. I have not heard any person say that there was anything wrong in them. They do not contain unsound advice and there is nothing wrong in these circulars, hut they happen to be signed by the deputy commissioner. The deputy commissioner happens to be a French Canadian. The wrong begins there. Is there anything wrong in these circulars ? If there is anything wrong I have not seen it. There are two circumstances which are taken advan-age of, and I say it boldly, face to face, to my hon. friends, that they should not take advantage of, as belonging to the other side of this House. The first is that Mr. CSte is a French Canadian. He has sent out these two circulars. In the second place 123
one of these circulars has been sent to the French Canadian priests. My hon. friends have insisted upon these two facts. It will not be to their political advantage, or to the advantage of men of their persuasion. Appeals to passion and prejudice do not last. They may help for a little time but they cannot last and as one who belonged for over twenty years to a great party, that was the Conservative party, I can say that it was not the policy of that party in former days. I say it proudly and I would ask, not only the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), in whom I have great confidence on that ground, but, those on the other side of the House who have political wisdom and experience, and I am calling upon them to-day not as a party man but as a Canadian, that they stop these appeals. Such appeals will not help them. They know that these appeals have been made. The hon. leader of the opposition will admit in his conscience and in his soul that the debate to-day has taken place upon this very ground.
No, no.
Yes. I appeal not only to those who are within the hearing of my voice but to those who will read these debates. It is because Mr. C0t6 is a French Canadian.
No, no.
Yes.
No, no.
Yes.
No, no.
Well, I would be glad to believe that I am wrong.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me a question ?
Certainly, with pleasure.

Is it only to-day that the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) knows of this feeling or is it not a fact that he has known of this feeling for the past year ? If this feeling has existed for the past year why did he not seek to allay it instead of appointing Mr. Cote, a French Canadian, to a new position ?

I do not understand what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) means by what he has said and nobody will understand. Mr. C0t6 has been engaged in political life ; he has never been accused by anybody of making appeals to passions and prejudices.
He is all right.
This debate has been brought up because
Mr. Cote happens to be a r rench Canadian and because
Some bon. MEMBERS. Oh, no.
I say yes. I give full credit to those who believe that I am wrong.
Will the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) permit me to ask him a question ?
Certainly.

Is it possible in this House to make an inquiry in regard to what may be a very legitimate and proper question without being charged with raising the racial cry ? If we cannot ask a proper question in this House without being accused of raising the racial question, surely all peace will depart from our deliberations and we cannot hope to give proper consideration to great questions.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS, t give full credit to the statement which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) has just made, and I am very glad of it. If I have spoken to-day on this point it is because, I must admit, that I was accused, myself, today, aud yesterday, in having dismissed about seventy-five workingmen from my de. partment of having acted as a Fi'ench Canadian and not as a minister obliged to keep only the men that he needs, but of having dismissed English Canadians and kept French Canadians. What are the facts'? They are just as simple as those in regard to these circulars. I have dismissed about sixty French Canadians and fifteen Englishspeaking Canadians. Read some of the Ontario Conservative newspapers.
An lion. MEMBER. Oh.

Yes, I read them this morning. I do not read them every day but I read them this morning. I am simply accused of having dismissed English-speaking Canadians. Well, in that very mechanical branch from which I dismissed fifteen men, the-English-speaking employees are still in a majority. I have conducted the Department of Public Works on broad lines.
Oh.
Yes, I say on broad lines.
Carried.
I want to prove it. Although it is well known, I want to prove it.
Hear, hear.
The chief accountant died and he was a French Canadian by the name of Dionne. I replaced him by an English Canadian. The chief architec' ;s an English Canadian.
Ob, dear, what a misfortune that is.
My hon. friends know that I am now just putting my finger on the nail that they have tried to put in my political coffin, but which they have not succeeded in driving in yet.

As the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has made an appeal to me, I venture to say a word in reply. If he should ask me as to whether I think there has been an attempt to raise a race cry here in the House, I would be inclined to refer him to his own remarks today. I thought that the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who sits in front of him dealt very fairly and very properly indeed with these questions to-day, and I earnestly hoped that the Minister of Public Works would have followed his leader's example, because if any person in the position of the Minister of Public Works will persist in flaunting words such as he has used to-day in the face of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House-a course that he has pursued more than once this session-he cannot be very desirous that these matters should be avoided as they ought to be avoided in this House. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has on at least two occasions during this session taunted me in a way that might have led me to retort, but I avoided doing so. I do not desire to make any retort now. I simply say in conclusion that I wish the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) had followed the example which was given him by his leader.

Mr. LaRIYIERE. I would call the attention of the hon. minister to the way these lists are printed. They are printed so close that except for reference they are no use at all. There is no margin in which to make any remarks or the signs necessary in checking them with the old lists, and the system of numbering the post offices is also very imperfect, because it changes from one polling booth to another polling booth, and the same number is never all through the lists. The polling booth lists of post offices are numbered at the head of the lists, and the lists are set in too small type. They should be set in columns with sufficient space between the names so that they could be used for other purposes than reference. It would be wise to make the lists in such a shape that they could be used not only for reference but at the polling booth when ever an election occurs. They have to be cut and pasted on other paper, and they are so closely set together that it is impossible to make a remark at either end of the names, unless written in such small letters that an ordinary man cannot read them. I would urge the government to change the system and have these lists printed in larger type and with sufficient space between the lines to enable us to use them for other purposes than reference.

I shall see that my hon. friend's suggestions are brought to the notice of the Secretary of State. We all desire that the lists should be made as useful as possible, and I hope his suggestions will be carried out.

The more one looks into it the less he is likely to understand the object of this circular that has been under discussion. At first it occurred to me that the object might be to make as favourable a showing as possible of the population of the province of Quebec, because the representation of other provinces is ascertained by dividing the population of Quebec by 65, the number of seats allowed to that province. But it will be seen that that could hardly have been the object, otherwise the circular would have been sent not merely to the French cures, but to the ministers of other denominations, for there must be a number of French people who do not belong to the Catholic Church. There are also residents of Quebec who are not of French extraction. Then, was it for the purpose of ascertaining the strength of the French race in the province ? That could hardly be. because we are told that the circular was sent to those districts in other provinces where there is large French settlements. Besides, there are French people in districts where there are no French priests, where there are Irish or German priests. I know some German priests, and it was not sent to them. It occurred to me that the object of the circular might be to ascertain the strength of the Roman Catholic Church. The fact that it was not sent to the German or Irish priests would hardly fit that theory. The thing is altogether inexplicable, unless the object was to ascertain the strength of the French element belonging to the Roman Catholic Church. That is the only explanation that suggests itself to my mind as at all probable. Whatever the explanation, it seems to be known only to the assistant commissioner and some of his friends who suggested this means of seeking to learn the strength of some element of the population.
These circulars were sent to other Catholic priests than the French.
That question was asked, and I understood, it was stated that the circular was sent only to the French Catholic priests.
I could not have heard the word ' French ' in the question if my answer conveyed that impression.
I know that it was sent to other Catholic priests besides the French. In my county there are Irish Catholic priests who received it.

Just before we rose at six o'clock, the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) was speaking. He used a very nice expression indeed-' we belong to the same Canadian nation.' I call the

members of this House to witness that while the hon. gentleman uses such expressions in the House, he fails to carry out the idea as he should. It has come to such a pass in this House that one can hardly speak of one who has the honour to belong to the French race and criticise him, but the Minister of Public Works is on his feet in a moment crying ' Race cry ! ' We have had more race cry from him this session than has been known for ten years before. And probably every day from now on we shall hear this taunt of ' race cry ' hurled across the floor whenever any hon. member criticises this government. I believe that ' We belong to the same Canadian nation;' and I believe that all Canadians should be treated the same, and not used as we have been by the sending out of these circulars, sent out by the Minister of Agriculture and marked ' confidential.' I have no objection to census enumerators getting all possible data concerning the French race. I believe that the French citizens, as a rule, are good citizens. But I believe that there should be no exception made. I care noc whether this gentleman's name is C8t6 or Blue or Brown, or anything else. It is not a question of name or race, but a question of equal usage of citizens in a country in which all citizens have equal rights.
It has been stated that this is because the French are a migratory race-if you will permit that term to be used. But they are not the only citizens of Canada that have that disposition. Take the maritime provinces, notwithstanding the statement that there has been no exodus from this Canada of ours, if you will stand at Vanceboro and Eastport, for any time during the past five or six years, you will see hundreds of citizens going to the New England states. They do not propose to make tlieir home there, but they go there during certain seasons of the year to find employment, and gravitate towards their home after the season is over. But there is no provision made for taking this class at all, they are not to be considered because they do not happen to he French. I know that in my own county, and no doubt in the county of Lunenburg and other counties in Nova Scotia, there is a class of persons who seek employment in the United States fishing fleet. But these people are not to be taken into consideration, it is only people to whom this confidential circular has been sent; and then, forsooth, because we call attention to it, we are accused of raising the race cry in this country. It is nearly time the Minister of Public Works, whom I regret to say I must hold accountable for a great deal of this trouble-I say it is pretty nearly time that he should bottle up that race cry of his and keei>
it at home, if he has any use for it. I am glad to see the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is present, *because I want to call his attention to an
instance that occurred in my county, of a gentleman of migratory instincts. He moved to the city of Eastport, and lived there for several years, enjoying all the advantages of citizenship under the United States flag. But things were not quite as happy as he would like to have them and he went away. His friends were good Reformers, and he applied for a position held by a good officer in the Fisheries Department. He was called home and was given the position. I made some inquiries about it. Perhaps the hon. gentleman may not be aware that he was not actually a voter in this country when they made him an officer; he was a voter in the United States. But that is the way this government prevents the exodus. They hunt up some poor fellow who has made the mistake of leaving this country, and they cajl him home and give him an office, dismissing some good officer to make him a position, although he may not even be a citizen of this country. Now, I think if the Minister of Agriculture had been frank and fair to this House, and had had these circulars printed in the Printing Bureau and fairly distributed in all the provinces among all the citizens, his action would have been commendable. But I can assure him that so far as the section of country from which I come is concerned, he wrill have the most severe censure.

A reference was made by the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Gagnon) to the proposed method to be employed by the Minister of Agriculture in taking the census. I want to say that in the county of Lunenburg which I have the honour to represent, as well as throughout the whole province of Nova Scotia, from Cape Sable to Cape North, there is a large migratory portion of the population who spend much of their time in fishing in the United States. I am anxious to know how such are to be placed, and in what industry they are to be classified. Are they to be lumped together as one industry and classified as such ? In my county I am happy to say that industry is more largely developed than in any other, and I think the number of fishermen will be found to be larger than in any other county.
Fishing is not called an industrial establishment. that terms does not apply to fishing at all.

But don't you think It should ? We have a number of industries connected with fishing on the shore in my county, such as curing fish, These people make their entire living in the fishing industry, and I think that ought to be counted as an industry, otherwise the resources of that province would not be fairly registered in the census to show that industry properly.

There is a special fishery schedule which deals with the fishing industry. But what we call industrial establishments would be such establishments as fish canneries or something like that. But men who go out to sea to fish do not come under that title at all.

I do not think it is fair to the fishermen who employ three, or four, or five, or ten men, and employ their capital, that they should not be looked upon as engaged in a certain industry. It is commonly called the fishing industry. I think the minister ought to make arrangements whereby instructions should be given to the enumerators to make a special list for that purpose.
We have a special schedule for that.

But the minister does not understand me. They would only be classed as one industry, and when a man employs several men, over five in number, to help him in the catch of fish or in the curing of fish, I think his business should be counted separately as an industry when the returns are made up by the enumerators. We have a number of other industries, such as boat-building, in which a great number of persons are employed in the winter time, and as soon as spring opens they seek employment in fishing. In the winter time there would be more than five men working together, and I think they should be counted as an industrial establishment.

There are special questions asking whether a person is occupied in one particular industry all the year round or only during a jjortion of the year, or if during a portion of the year they are occupied in another industry, and the time they devote to each.

The minister will see, then, that they are shut out from being classified as forming one of the industries. I think that is unfair. The same with barrel-making. A large number of barrels are being made to serve as packages for fish, and those engaged in this employment should be counted in the same way an industry.
They are.
But, they are not known as industries, and I contend that they should be counted as such. I think they should have recognition in that way.

I think the hon. gentleman is misrepresenting the word ' industries ' as we have been using it. WTe have been talking about industrial establishments which I take to be manufacturing establishments. Every occupation is an industrial one, and, in the Mr. KAULBACH.

The population of the province of Quebec is the basis upon which is calculated the representation of the other provices in the Dominion parliament. The constitution Axes at sixty-five the number of our representatives in the House of Commons. If the census determines that our population is 1,750,000, that number divided by sixty-five, the number of our representatives, will give an average of 26,922 per representative. If Ontario, for example, has a population of 2,250,000, that number divided by 26,922 will give eighty-three, which will be the number of its representatives in the Commons. Actually it is ninety-two, so that it would lose nine representatives.
That is the programme laid out by Le Soleil, the organ of the Liberal party in the city of Quebec, and I call it to the attention of my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule), who was in such a dilemma a short time ago.
