The Conservative party-and I do not accuse the whole Conservative party, let my words be well understood, because I know that there are In the Conservative ranks a great many men who do not approve of the dangerous policy to which some gentlemen from the other side have resorted-but I say that the Conservative party will never come back to office unless they make up their minds to give up that policy. The French Canadians will not be alone to keep them out of office. There will be a reaction, a powerful, generous reaction in the English population, among the very men that may have been misled by those appeals. We

are not going to stand idle. I do not speak as a party man. I do not know how long my health will permit me to remain in the position I occupy.' This is not a party question, but I cannot express too deeply my sorrow and regret when I hear, and when I see

Some lion. MEMBERS. Oh, oh.

There may be some gentlemen who do not understand the meaning of what I say, but I say that I cannot express too deeply my regret when I see this young Canadian nation, which is called to such a high destiny, exposed to grave perils by appeals of that kind. We have had difficulties in the past, we have been obliged to change our form of government nearly every thirty years. Why ? Because the two races did not seem able to agree. Those hon. gentlemen who are conducting this racial campaign are simply leading us to some deadlock. I ask those who have laughed to reflect a little. I say that the Conservative party is going back on the policy they followed for a long time, and which was successful, and until they make up their minds to change their present ways and methods they do not deserve to come back to office.
And they will not.
And they will not.

The hon. Minister of Public Works is smarting under the discovery of his own acts and his own schemes, inimical to the well-being of confederation; and true to his old instincts and practices, he attempts to raise a cloud in order to escape from it, and I will not permit him to do so just now. He tells us about North Bruce and how he found matters there. It is no wonder that the gentleman who was going to show the Ontario leaders of the party how to run an election and who came back to this House like a whipped spaniel, should feel pretty sore at finding that the machinations and means that carried elections in other places were of no use in the north riding of Bruce. Now, as to the speech I made in British Columbia I do not retract a line or a word of it. The hon. gentleman says I made attacks upon the French Canadian. If you attack the hon. Minister of Public Works and say that his record is a record of dishonesty, you are, according to that hon. gentleman, attacking the whole French Canadian race. If you say that Bourassa and Monet are traitors to the country, you are attacking the whole French Canadian race. I said in this House last year that these two men were traitors to Canada. And the right hon. First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), if not in so many words, said the same thing
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon
Not in so many words, perhaps, but the whole of his argument

Order.
ilr. WALLACE. The whole of his argument was in that direction, and yet he would take them to-morrow to his bosom.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) is mistaken. I said nothing of the kind. Mr. Bourassa is entitled to his opinions, which are not mine. But the views that he expressed have been expressed on the floor of the House of Commons of England.

No, Sir. He expressed some views that have been expressed on the floor of the House of Commons in England, but he expressed some views that would not be expressed by any loyal man in this country. He abused our troops, and did everything that a disloyal man would do, and I characterized him and Monet-I beg his pardon for mentioning his -name, the member for Laprairie-I characterized them as traitors. And I would like to know from the Minister of Public Works if, because you find some men on that side of the House who are disloyalists and traitors to their country, or, if you attack the Minister of Public Works you are therefore attacking two millions of French Canadians ? I think it is about time that humbug of that sort should cease. I do not withdraw a. word of what I said, nor shall I do so. The hon. gentleman said further that I characterized them as Frenchmen first and that he had made a speech in the province of Quebec saying that they were Frenchmen first. I would like him to say if that were not true.
Let him go on. I am going to answer him in good form.

I have a report here taken from the Montreal Star of the 22nd of September of 1899. It is a report of the annual dinner of the law students of Laval. Mr. Justice Wurtele and Mr. Monk spoke. The hon. Minister of Public Works also spoke, and among other things he said-and this is given in quotation marks indicating a verbatim report of that por-tlon of his speech ;
One of the paramount duties of the French members of the House of Commons was to show that they were Frenchmen. _ We were happy to he British subjects, as this fact also-permitted us to remain French Canadians.
I say so again.

I said in British Columbia, and I say here again to-night, that,
in my opinion the paramount duty of the-

392S
French member of the House of Commons and of tlie English-speaking member as well was to be a Canadian, and a British Canadian. I say that language of the kind I have just read is utterly uncalled for, that it is calculated to create dissention and division which a loyal citizen of this country would seek to avoid, but the hon. Minister of Public Works Is repeating it with variations on every possible occasion. What about the interview in France at the Paris exposition last year ? It is true that last year the right hon. First Minister said :	I am not responsible for reports appearing in newspapers, I shall wait until I hear more authentic reports of the hon. minister's utterances. Has he received more authentic reports ? Who sent out the report which appeared in La Patrie, a paper belonging to the hon. minister or his family? Was it not the hon. Minister of Public Works himself ? Did lie not say in the interview :	We have to disguise our feelings ?
I never said such a thing in my life.

I am giving the substance of what the hon. minister said. I have the article in my possession, but have not it under my hand at this moment. But 1 know that this whole country was shocked and surprised that a minister of the Crown from Canada should make such statements in a foreign country, giving aid and comfort to those who were at any rate not friendly to Great Britain at that'parti-cular time when the mother country needed all her sous to stand to her aid. That was the position of the hon. minister, and that position I protested against and shall continue to protest against as long as I am in this House or out of it, and able to enter a protest. Everything I said in British Columbia I repeat. These men, in my opinion, are traitors to their country. I hold the opinion to-day that I did then about the Minister of Public Works, making a speech to the students of Laval University and preaching that the par-mount duty of a French member of the House of Commons was to show that they were Frenchmen. What about our Canadian citizenship ? Are we to have no Canadians in this country, are we to have no British subjects in this country, that it must be their paramount duty to be French Canadians ? Why not British Canadians ? Why not Canadians without any prefix, if that will suit him better ? We are all Canadians; we ought all to be loyal Canadians. But I say that this attitude of the minister and this attitude of the gentleman to whom I have alluded is an attitude, in my opinion detrimental and injurious to the best interests of this country. As to these circulars, the hon. gentleman says that the whole murder is out. and that I have made a speech. Well, I made a few remarks, and he was Mr. WALLACE.
not able to point out anything that I said that was not correct. He says that he will herald what I have said in the province of Quebec. I am told that every issue of his paper for months had my name in it as an Orangiste, as he calls it, as if it was a crime to be an Orangeman, to belong to an association incorporated by this parliament under an Act signed by the Governor General as representative of Her Majesty, an association whose principles no man can impugn, those principles being loyalty to the country and the institutions under which we live, unswerving and unwavering loyalty. That is the crime that I am charged with in the province of Quebec, and the hon. gentleman thinks he is justified in saying : Oh, Wallace, is an Orangeman, and therefore he is unfit to be a representative of the people, he is unfit for any position. Mr. Chairman, the man who was First Minister of Canada for a longer period than any other man, was an Orangeman ; the Hon. J. J. C. Abbott, another premier of Canada, was an Orangeman ; the Hon. Sir Mackenzie Bowell, another premier of Canada, was an Orangeman. There are three premiers of Canada since confederation who were members of the Orange Association. Was it ever charged that it was a crime for them to belong to that association ? That is the charge made by the Minister of Public Works in his newspaper, attempting thereby to gain political advantage by using the cry that I am an Orangeman, and that not only I should be condemned myself, but the political party to which I belong should be condemned also. Now, I say, judging by the course that has been taken by the Minister of Public Works, it looks as if he were the party who sent out this circular. Some one writes to me and says :
I am told C6te, when employed at Ottawa, was correspondent of La Patrie, Tarte's paper.
That may be true, or untrue, the Minister of Public Works can tell. We all know it is correct, anyway. That was printed and sent out without the knowledge of the Minister of Agriculture. But does anybody tell me it was sent out without the knowledge of the Minister of Public Works, who we know, from experience and observation, takes charge whenever he chooses of everybody's department in the whole government ? We find him day by day, without the slightest hesitation, chiming in and dominating and dictating to every minister, and therefore we can easily believe that the Minisfer of Public Works had something to do with the publication of these two confidential circulars. But he says they were not confidential because they were sent out to thousands of people. Does he tell me that the one sent to the curds in the province of Quebec marked ' confidential,' was not a confidential circular ? He says it was a mistake. How does he know it was a mistake ? Where did he learn it was a mistake ?

By what authority does he tell us it was a mistake ?
The MINISTER O'F PUBLIC WORKS. The minister said that himself.
The minister did not know anything about it until after the circulars were out. Does the Minister of Public Works say that he did not know anything about it until the circulars were out ?
I did not know that they were published till I read them in the papers.
He did not know they were published till he read them.
In the papers.

When did that occur ? Well, then, I say that if Mr. Cdt6, without the authority of the Minister of Public Works, and without the authority of the Minister of Agriculture, has violated the regulations which he was bound to uphold, by sending out a private and confidential circular to a portion of the population, he grossly violated his duty. The Minister of Public Works says that this young Canadian nation is exposed to perils by appeals- such as he made to this House himself tonight. He is making these appeals continually, it is his whole stock-in-trade, and if he could not make these appeals his occupation and his usefulness to his political party would be gone. I say that we are exposed to. great perils and dangers, and we are exposed to these perils and dangers because of the Minister of Public Works and his utterances on all occasions of this kind. He says in another place :
I am a minister in a British government. I have liberty to call myself French, but if it is desired that I should declare myself a British citizen, and if it is desired to prevent me calling myself French, then I refuse to call myself a British subject. We are happy and free under British institutions, but France is also my dear mother country.
Canada is mine, that is the difference between us two.
I am sorry for Canada.

Well, Canada has a good deal to be sorry for, and If it had no more loyal sons than the one who made the interruption, I would say, God help Canada. He says also, when the war was going on last year :
What have we to do with things in Africa? Why should we take the money and blood of our people to spend them in such far-away regions?
He did not do very much in that direction himself. He does not need to make any boast of his efforts in that behalf, because if there was any one who discouraged and discredited any effort in that direction, it
was the Minister of Public Works and those two young men behind him whom he inspired with the same ideas that he had himself in this regard, with the same Ideas that I have just read as a reflex of the mind of the Minister of Public Works, so far as he dares to give voice to his opinions. Now, Sir, for myself I shall not be a party to any disloyalty In this country so long as I live. I shall not be one who will coquette with a foreign country and disparage his own. My loyalty is due to the old flag that we live under, to the King who reigns over us, and to the Dominion of Canada, the proudest part of the great British Empire.

The hon. gentleman has stated that I have not done much in the war in South Africa. I want to know when he has been killed for the King. I want to know how much blood he has shed, and where it is. Now, I am always amused when I see a gentleman exalting his own loyalty.
I can tell the hon. gentleman that a son of mine was out there, and did his duty by his flag. I do not think there were any Tartes there.

Well, I compliment the hon. gentleman on the fact that his son has come back in good health, and I compliment him on the fact that his son went there. The fact that one of his sons went to the front does not prove that my sons are' not just as loyal as his son. ,We were not all at liberty to go out there. Besides, there are members in this government who have sent their sons, some of whom have been killed.
I made no comparison till I was challenged to do so.

The hon. gentleman better possess his mind in peace. The fact that he is always speaking of his loyalty does not prove that other men are not as loyal as he is. He has stated, not only in British Columbia, but all over Ontario, that the French Canadians are not loyal. I pass over what he may have said about myself.

I deny that I have ever made such a statement as that. I stated that individuals such as the hon. Minister of Public Works were not loyal, but he says the French Canadian race. I repudiate that statement again.

The hon. gentleman makes a statement on the floor of parliament, and I am bound to accept it, and I do accept it, but, I have read his speech. I have just read one in which he says that the loyalty of the French is lip loyalty. I have read his speech. If he says he has not made that speech I will accept his statement without any hesitation. I accept statements from any hon.

gentleman when they are made on the floor of parliament. But, he has made that speech and he has made it publicly, not on the floor of parliament, but he has made It, it has been read all oyer the country, and it is not the first speech of the kind that he has made. The fact that he has made these speeches explains why he has not been able to satisfy his ambition to occupy the chair that the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Borden) is occupying to-day. Now, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) has proved the contrary of what he is trying to establish. He has alluded to the fact that Sir John Abbott and Sir Mackenzie Bowell belonged to the Orange Order. These gentlemen have been supported by the province of Quebec, which knew very well that they belonged to the Orange Order, but, in the Orange Order, there are men and men as there are in every other class of the community. There are men that we are bound to respect in the Orange Order, and there are those that we are bound to judge as we see fit. The hon. gentleman has never known a word of the French language. I do not make it a crime to him, but, all the same he does not know a word of French, and he is quoting my interviews and speeches made in French. I say, without any hesitation, that he is quoting speeches and words that X have never uttered. I ask to be judged, not upon the misquotations that have been read both inside and outside of parliament, but, I am prepared to stand by every word that I qttered both in France and here. I never said in France that we were disguising our views, but that we had to act with discretion. I have seen published in the Conservative press things that I never said in my life.
And in La Patrie too.
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) read La Patrie ? He has not that good fortune, I am sorry to say. He has read quotations that have been cooked for political purposes.
By Cartwright.

There is nothing easier in the world than to distort the words of a gentleman who speaks in French when you report them in English. There is this to be said, and to this I call the attention not only of this parliament, but of all those fair-minded men in the province of Ontario, that in Ontario the French Canadian newspapers are not read. Our English friends do not read the French newspapers. Then, it is the easiest possible thing for a dishonest newspaper man, and there are very few, I hope, to distort the words and meaning of the speeches of a public man. I say, without hesitation, that I have never uttered the speeches and words that were reported Mr. TARTE.
in the Tory press during the last campaign. There could not have been more misrepresentation under the sun than during the last campaign. Whether I stay here, as a minister, or whether I go into private life, I will make it my duty and pleasure to go to the province of Ontario to be judged by what I shall say and by what I have said, I have said somewhere that I would be glad to have a discussion with the leaders of the Orange Order, with the hon. gentleman himself. I have so much confidence in the fairness of our English friends when they are face to face with these men that I would be glad to have a discussion with the leaders of the Orange Order. A French Canadian who is right in his views, who is a loyal British citizen, need not fear to go to Ontario. I have said in France what I have repeated over and over again here, that the French Canadians were happy and contented under British rule. What I have said there is true. Will you permit me to add that the French Canadians are more interested in being loyal than their friends of British origin. We cannot go anywhere else. If this country were annexed to the United States we would be altogether drowned. We would rather remain under the British flag than under any other state of affairs. Why should we not be loyal then, Sir ? Our hearts are loyal just as much as if our interests alone dictated to us to be loyal. We enjoy the same liberties as our English friends enjoy, and I say that it is a crime against the happiness and future of this nation to brand as disloyal nearly one-third of the population. It is a crime, and I denounce that crime. The hon. gentleman knows that he is guilty of having branded us as disloyal men. He knows it, his friends know it, and his party know it. He has branded us as a disloyal race, but he would not dare to say that on the floor of parliament when the whole nation is listening. He would say that in some corner of the land. He would not state that here, but, he has never repudiated his statement.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. I understood the hon. member for West York (Mr. Wallace) to emphatically deny that he had made such a statement, and the minister was good enough to say that he accepted the hon. gentleman's denial.
I accepted it.
The hon. gentleman repeats the same thing.

Before I sit down, I just want to call the attention of the committee and of hon. gentlemen on both sides to the methods tnat are adopted by some of our Tory friends. I dismissed 75 men a few days ago when

the department did not require them anymore. We have no more work. Firemen and engineers for the heating system are not required at the present moment. We dismissed a lot of them. Out of those dismissed, there were, if 1 remember rightly, about fifteen or sixteen English-speaking men. The balance, about sixty, or in the neighbourhood of that, were French Canadians. Now, the Citizen, the very morning after these dismissals, called attention to the fact that fifteen Englishmen had been dismissed from the mechanical branch, not mentioning, of course, the fact that sixty French Canadians had been dismissed elsewhere. Now, let me read to you from the Hamilton Spectator :
Mr. Tarte has again been bridging over the yawning gulf between the British and French people of Canada by slandering the former. Last week he dismissed seventy employees of the Public Works Department. In the mechanical department thirteen out of the fifteen discharged were English-speaking mechanics. Questioned about it in the House, Mr. Tarte affirmed that this discrepancy was merely incidental to the policy of dismissing inferior and retaining superior workmen. In other words, Mr. Tarte says that French Canadian mechanics are superior to British Canadian mechanics ! Thus the master of the Grit administration adds insult to injury.
Now, I leave this country to judge of the methods that are adopted to raise prejudices against me. It is. not against me that these appeals are made. I am a very humble citizen of this country, and it is not against me, personally, but it is against me, because I am a French Canadian.

No.
Other hon. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

If an English Minister of Public Works had dismissed these men that article would not have been written, but I have been branded all over Ontario as a French Canadian who hates the English population. My fellow-countrymen of French origin have been accused of being disloyal ; of being an inferior race, of being a conquered race. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) will not deny that he has. over and over again, called us a conquered race. All over Ontario everything I do is qualified in a way to try and show that, of course, I boss the whole administration ; that I hold the right lion, the Prime Minister in my right hand, the hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce in my left hand, the Minister of Railways and Canals In my right pocket, and all my other colleagues in my hat. They try to make out that the whole business is in my hands, and being a bad Frenchman, that I am a terrible man for the English population. That is just what it means. When I go to Ontario some good Conservatives who met me in past days look at me and exclaim : How is it that Tarte changed so much.
They look at me to see if I have horns or some other infernal implements about me. I am very sorry, Mr. Chairman, that so much time has been taken up in this debate, hut, it is not my fault. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) appears to have made up his mind that I wrote those circulars myself, and printed and circulated them myself, but I give the House my word that I only read them for the first time when I read them in the newspapers.
Mr. Chairman, I thought the question 'before the House was the granting of money to take the census ?
Hear, hear.
We have been treated all the afternoon by both parties to personal abuse, and if this is the way you manage business in the parliament of Canada, I think I will have to resign.
Oh, no.

Well, I can never stand that kind of thing. I have heard more personal abuse since I have been in this parliament than I ever heard in all the associations I ever attended in my life. The language that has been thrown across the floor this afternoon and evening is an insult to the people of Canada. I feel as though I would like to introduce a Bill in which I would provide that every individual who brings up this racial cry should be fined $100, and put in tbe tower for a period of
Twelve months.
Any man who introduces anything that would hurt the feelings of his neighbour on this side of the House, or on that side, should be imprisoned in the tower for a month at any rate.
Hear, hear.

If the Prime Minister allows me, I will introduce that Bill. It is about titae that we people no matter from whom we sprung, should learn how to behave ourselves on this continent, where we have all the privileges and all the advantages of a happy people. But, 'still some people come here and bicker at each other and fight like dogs. It is a shame that we should bring these things up in the parliament of Canada. Let us go on with the business, and pass the accounts, and get home by bed time.
I just want to ask the minister if he has received any replies to the telegram sent out by him in reference to the political circular that was distributed throughout Ontario ?
Will the minister give the names of the nine who admit they did have it, as well as the other three ?

I do not think I have the names of the com-missoners, but I have the names of the electoral districts : Algoma (Fort William) ; Algoma (Port Arthur) ; North Bruce (one) ; West Bruce, Cardwell, North Essex, South Grey, West Middlesex, and Toronto West. These were the constituencies in which it had been seen, but not used, as far as the commissioners had any information or could find out. There were three in which it had been received, and had been in the hands of the enumerators more or less : North York, North Hastings and East Northumberland, and in these it was immediately followed up and destroyed.
Would the minister lay these papers on the Table of the House ?
This is a mere statement, but I will lay copies of the replies on the Table.
That is what I mean.

It will he refreshing to the people of Ontario to know that in North York, represented by the Hon. Mr. Davis in the local legislature, there are such appearances of fright as to call upon that gentleman to use the enumerators for this purpose. It is quite gratifying to us on this side of the House to have the statement made ; but, it would be much more satisfactory, not only to us, but I have no doubt to the people of Ontario and the rest of the Dominion, to know now what steps the minister has taken to have the matter thoroughly sifted, and to find out from whom these circulars passed to the census commissioners and the enumerators. Have any steps been taken in that regard ?

No steps have been taken except to prevent the use by the enumerators of any schedules not issued by the department. I may say, from information that has come to me from the same source as that which has come to bon. gentlemen opposite, namely, the public press, that I notice various statements to the effect that the circular in question is one which has been issued by the political organization in the province of Ontario for the purpose of organizing for the revision of the voters' lists. Apparently that circular has been sent out to the chiefs of that organization in the different parts of the province. Apparently three of these chiefs, or somebody acting for them, in some way which I do not know or care about, got the circulars into the hands of the census enumerators in those three districts, and they apparently began to use them. That improper action on the part of the enumerators has been stopped, and anything they did in connection with them has been destroyed.
Will the hon. minister say whether he dismissed those officials or not ? because he promised that he would.
I said that I would dismiss any who refused to do what they were instructed to do.
I want to know if you dismissed those three enumerators, as you promised to dismiss any who used these circulars.
I have not, because the moment they were ordered to do so they destroyed them, and fulfilled their instructions.
Will the hon. gentleman he kind enough to read the first section of his report-the precise language he used- because I did not catch it ?
I said that in 102 cases out of the 114 the census commissioners reported that they knew nothing of the circular and had found no trace of it in their ridings.
Is that the language the hon. gentleman used before ?

The language varies according to the replies of the commissioners. I cannot quote the language in every instance. Nine replied that they had heard of those schedules, but that they had not been used, and there were three who reported that apparently some of the enumerators had used them, and in these cases the commissioners immediately destroyed them, or ordered them to be destroyed where they did not do it personally.

The most startling statement made by the minister was that he did not care anyway, as to the action of these gentlemen in having these circulars in their keeping ; in other words, that nothing was going to be done.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I did not say I did not care about their having them in their keeping. I said I did not know how they had reached them and did not care.

Well, that is 'a most startling proposition. The hon. gentleman appoints a large ' number of gentlemen throughout the Dominion to take the census returns. These in turn have a number of persons appointed under them, no doubt on the recommendation of the member or the defeated candidate for the riding ; these men who are acting as enumerators are sworn not to divulge any information they may receive in that capacity. Immediately after they are appointed some person unknown to us at the present time goes to them and deliberately asks them to do, what? To violate their oath and give him information so that when the courts of revision are coming on for the approaching elections in Ontario, they will be fortified with all the facts ; and the minister stands up now and says lie does not care what they do.
I did not say that.
The hon. gentleman said a moment ago that it concerned him to no extent further.
The hon. gentleman is misquoting me entirely. I stated that I did not know who put them into their hands and I did not care who did so.

I want nothing stronger than that. The hon. gentleman says that although these census enumerators have been supplied with these forms, and although they have been asked to commit what is nothing more nor less than subornation of forgery, he does not care-it is no concern of his whether or not this attempt has been made to tamper with the census enumerators. The minister the other night, when 124
this was brought home to him and he saw the force of it, was so panic-stricken that before he left the House he caused to be sent to all the enumerators a telegram telling them that if these circulars were being used they were at once to be destroyed ; and I think ' Hansard ' will bear out that he promised to have any dismissed who were found using them. Some of them have been found using them. I have under my hand a case in North Simcoe, where the enumerator says : 'I have seen the schedule referred to, but it is not in circulation here.' But Mr. Curry, who is the enumerator, must know who supplied him with those forms, and the House and the country will expect to be informed, because whoever supplied them was asking him to do an illegal act. The minister tells us in effect that this is a matter of no concern to him at all, although the other night he assured the House that the matter would be probed to the hilt, and he would find out who was guilty of wrongdoing. Will the minister tell the House before the item passes whether he intends to have an inquiry in order to ascertain who supplied the enumerators with these forms, how many committed a breach of confidence by using them, and after that, if an investigation shall prove that any of these men have any of these forms in their possession, and have been using them, what he proposes to do ?

As I said a few minutes ago, my information leads me to believe that this schedule or circular or form for political organization purposes was prepared by the political organization in the province of Ontario, and was distributed to the leading men of that organization in the different ridings. Just to what extent I do not know; I do not think it boots that I should know. In a few instances they were seen and known of by the census commissioners. The reply from North Simcoe, which the hon. gentleman has just quoted, says that the census commissioner had seen the circular. He does not say that he had seen it in connection with his census work, but he says it was not used in census work. I do not know how many commissioners or enumerators may have seen this circular. It matters not to me in my administration whether they have seen it or not, so long as they do not make any use of it, or in any way prostitute their office in my department in the use of it ; and from the information and replies which I have received, it Is evident that there have been only three constituencies in the whole province where any such thing has occurred. And in those places, the wrong has been completely stopped under the orders I have issued. I do not therefore see any necessity for departmental inquiry as to where this paper came from.
What three counties were these ?
North York, North Hastings, and East Northumberland. The commissioners there represented that they had found a fetv of those circulars and had immediately caused them to be destroyed.
What is the circular which the minister found in the hands of some of his enumerators ? Did the hon. gentleman take any steps to procure that circular and will he lay it on the Table of the House?
Tlie hon. the loader of the opposition read it in the House the other night, and that was the first I ever saw. That and the one which is in my office are all I have ever seen.	.
Where did the hon. gentleman get the one which is in his office ?
I found it on the table in my desk. 1 think it was sent by one of those gentlemen in the constituencies I have named.

How many used it ?
The MINISTER OF AGRIOo-* uRE. Three. There were nine others who said they had seen it or known of its existence, but had not used it, and I think it is one of them who sent a copy to me.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Are the words ' the Dominion of Canada ' endorsed on the back of the one in the hon. gentleman's office ?
I have not got it here and cannot tell the hon. gentleman. The one I have is the same as the one which the leader of the opposition read.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That circular purports to come from the Dominion of Canada and not from Ontario, and does not appear to have been got up by a political party for use in the province of Ontario alone.
I was not aware that those words were endorsed on the back.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The papers that were put into the hands of the enumerators were endorsed ' Dominion of Canada ' and purported to be official documents coming from here. Since this document was found in the hands of the minister's officers, he should find out who perpetrated that forgery. The minister cannot expect this item to pass until he furnishes all the information. The Reform papers came out a few days ago saying this was a trick played by the Conservative party. The Globe tried to throw the blame on the Conservative party, but now wre are going to get at the bottom of this thing. It was found by three commissioners who say that it was all over the constituency in the hands of the enumerators. The right hon. the Mr. INGRAM.
Prime Minister has said that Ontario is his right arm, and we find that the hon. Mr. Ross sent down his confidential man to be the census commissioner at Ottawa and do what he could to prevent this government losing, its right arm. And what then do we find ? We find a document placed in tlie hands of the enumerators, printed somewhere-the Minister of Agriculture says he does not know where and does not care to know anything about it-and that is the document concerning which we are determined to find out everything before this item is allowed to pass. We have succeeded in acquitting the Conservative party of the charge made that this was a trick played by them to get the department into a scrape, because the minister admits that the whole thing was got up by the Reform Association in Toronto. What right has that association to publish documents endorsed ' Dominion of Canada ' and purporting to be one of the census documents ? The minister tells us innocently that he does not know where they came from, but he is not doing his duty unless he finds out where >and by whom the fraud was perpetrated, and if it was committed through the connivance of one of his commissioners, that official should be dismissed.

All the information I have is what appears in the public press. I read a letter in the Toronto Globe about a week ago, which was signed Alex. Smith, and which stated what this circular was and why and how it was issued. That Is all the information I have about it. The hon. gentleman insinuates that my officers are responsible.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Certainly, they were found in the hands of your officers.

I have stated positively that my department had no knowledge of it and is in no way responsible. It has nothing -whatever to do with the census work. And where, in a few7 instances, it has been found in the hands of enumerators, it has been placed there without the connivance or authority or knowledge of the department at Ottawa or of the census commissioner. And the moment it was found in the hands of a few enumerators-only three in the province of Ontario-it was immediately suppressed by my orders and destroyed. As to the way in which it got into the hands of the commissioners I have no means of knowing.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That is what we want to know.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) may want to know. I cannot control his wants in the matter. I do not think it matters to the administration of my department how it came to be in their hands, provided the use

[DOT]of it has been stopped and their utilization of any knowledge therein has been stopped or prevented. The statement that I referred to in the Globe is practically the same as that I made a few moments ago, that this circular was issued, as a good many others have Been, by the Liberal organizations of the province of Ontario, that it was issued in the different ridings all over the province so that they might get the information for the purpose of properly revising the voters' lists. In some instances, apparently, the officers of the organization in the various ridings have communicated with the census commissioners. In some instances, the census commissioners have said they could not and would not use it or have anything to do with it. If there were ridings in which it got into the hands of enumerators, the use of it by them has been suppressed, and any information got by enumerators has been destroyed. Under these circumstances, I do not think it is necessary, as a departmental matter of administration, that there should be any further investigation.

It seems to me that the minister is not doing his whole duty in stopping there. Either the census enumerators have been imposed upon, or they have been doing what was in violation of their oath of secrecy. The hon. gentleman admits that it was used in some localities. Surely, it would be his duty to ascertain from his commissioners or enumerators if he can, from what source they received it, or whether they have used it. And, if they have used it, it must be as he admits, in violation of their oath. And, in that case surely he will try to inflict some punishment upon them for violation of their oath of duty.
What was the date of the telegram sent by the hon. minister ?
The 15th of April, about 11 o'clock at night.

And a number of these replies are dated on the morning of the 16th
at 10 o'clock. Will the hon. gentleman inform us how a census commissioner living at one end of his riding, receiving a telegram sent at that time, could get the information that none of the enumerators were using that circular, and send back a statement to that effect by 10 o'clock on the morning of the 16th.
He probably knew what his enumerators were doing.

Let me give a couple of illustrations. Here is the answer from South Norfolk. That very large county. It would be impossible for the census commissioner to be able to procure from the different enumerators a response to any re-1244
quest that might be made informing him that they were not using that circular. Then here is the reply from the county of Peel, the county I have the honour to represent. This telegram says, ' I have written you.' And it says also, ' I know nothing about the circular.' That means that on the morning of the 16th, the earliest time when this gentleman could receive this telegram, he sits down immediately and writes an answer to the telegram of the hon. minister. And I suppose in the letter that he writes he says that the circular is not being used in the county of Peel. Let me tell the hon. minister that the census commissioner for Peel lives at the extreme northern boundary of the county, and that it is 26 miles to the southern boundary. If the commissioner was attending properly to his duties, it would be impossible for him to receive answers from these enumerators in the county at once. Therefore, I say that the telegrams are not sufficient information that this cirucualr had not been used, particularly as the minister has made the statement that he had found them in use in three different counties in Ontario. But what I would like the hon. minister to do is to give his opinion as to how these gentlemen could get the information upon which to base these telegrams sent on the morning of the 16 th.

In the first place, I would say that I find that after the question came up here before, this matter was in the newspapers of Toronto. This was several days before the telegram was sent from here. The matter appears to have been in the minds of some of the commissioners, and some of the replies show that they had already made investigation. I suppose they investigated on this newspaper report, and before my telegram of the 15th reached them. I cannot say exactly as to the answer from Peel, as I do not remember the details of each reply. I went over each reply. The statement of the commissioners that no such circular had been received in their districts, I accepted, because I am confident they would not say it if it was not correct.
Would the hon. minister lay the letter from the Peel commissioner upon the Table ?

Yes. Evidently from that telegram there is a letter. I received other letters supplementary to the telegrams, and I thought they were on the file handed to the hon. gentleman; but the letter does not appear to be there. The letters I received in elucidation of the telegram must have been confirmatory, otherwise I would have so stated. The telegram stated the facts in regard to the matter, and there is no letter contradictory to the telegram or giving a different meaning.
Could the hon. gentleman state about liow many enumerators there would be in an average county of the province of Ontario ?
There is an enumerator for each polling division, I could not tell what the number is.

In the county of Peel there would be twenty-five enumerators that this gentleman would have to see. He receives a telegram on the morning of the 16th ; he sits down and answers by letter and sends a telegram confirming the letter, and I suppose the inference is that he has consulted the whole twenty-five in the county, in the twenty-five different sections of the county, at work in twenty-five different farm-houses, I suppose. Does the hon. gentleman think that this information is a sufficient answer to his telegram ?

I take it that when the census commissioner makes me a plain statement he has ground to justify that statement, and would not make it unless he knew what he was stating. I said a moment ago that this matter was in the public press of Toronto for several days before it was taken up in this House, and it had even been referred to in the legislature of Toronto. I have no doubt that among the census commissioners there were some who, as they stated in these replies, before they received my telegram, had investigated the matter and had found no trace of the circular. I dare say the census commissioner in Peel had discussed the matter and found out about it before he sent that telegram. But that is only a supposition. But I take it that when he sent the telegram stating there were none in use, that he knew what he was talking about.
Will the minister be good enough to lay on the Table the form of oath that was required to be taken by the enumerators ?
It was laid on the Table several days ago.
I have been unable to find it. Perhaps the minister will tell me where I may find it.
The form of oath was laid on the Table since the discussion arose some days ago, and the clerk knows where it is.

I assume the form of oath is in accordance with the law. Now, the law clearly states that none of the special enumerators shall secure information other than that required by the census schedules. I am clear that there is no instruction in the schedules to obtain the ages of every person between the years of 16 and 21. Is it an instruction to the enumerators to secure the names of all parties between 16 and 21 ?
It is an Instruction to the enumerators to secure the age of everybody they put down.

The hon. gentleman has not answered the question. If there is any such instruction, I challenge the minister to produce it. Now, what was the position of this whole matter ? Knowing that the Ontario elections were coming on, knowing that next fall the courts of revision would be held, which wTere of vital import to the Ontario government, they go to work and some person belonging to the Liberal organization issues a circular which is passed around among the enumerators, and this circular invites these men to commit a breach of the law, after they have taken a solemn oath that they will not divulge to any person the information they have obtained. These men, by this circular, are asked to commit perjury in giving him the ages of all persons between 16 and 21. What was the object ? The object was this : When the courts -were going on this fall the Liberals would be in a position to know who to apply to have struck off on the Conservative side who were not 21, and in that way they will not be put to the expense of subpoenaing witnesses and bringing them to court. Now, the minister says to-night that he feels his duty has been carried out, that having found out who were the wrongdoers and the assurance from them that they are not going to carry it out any further, that is an end of the matter. I ask the minister this question : Assuming that one of his enumerators had by chance laid down his book, and some person had walked off with it and got certain information from it and then returned the book, and it came to the knowledge of the minister that this party' had had access to his book, would not the minister have felt called upon to punish that party ? Certainly he would, and if party pressure had been brought to bear to cause an illegal action of that kind, I am bound to say that the minister would have been very vigorous in bringing the guilty party to punishment. Yet. when the minister finds that certain parties have been doing this illegal act, after having taken the oath that they will not furnish the information, the minister washes his hands of the whole matter and thinks that it is not a question to be dealt with seriously. The minister did not propose to treat the matter in such a cavalier way the other night. He found the effect of the Ross attempt to laugh the matter out of court, so to speak. He found that the Montreal Witness and other newspapers had reprimanded and reprobated the conduct of Mr. Ross, and the hon. gentleman was not prepared to be as flippant as Mr. Ross was. I won't say that he connived at the commission of this offence, but when the offence had been proved he attempted to

make light of it. But before the minister left the building that night, what did we find him doing ? Industriously telegraphing from one end of the province of Ontario to the other to find where this document was. The minister felt the seriousness of the position, and before he left the House that night he said this :
I have stated before and I state again that if anything has been done beyond the law and the requirements of the duties of the enumerators, they will be brought to task, and it will be seen by me as head of the department under which they are working that they do their work legally, lawfully and properly, according to the strict letter of the law which lays down their duties.
Now, are they going to be brought to task ? Were these mere empty words to kill time that the minister used when he [DOT]said he was going to bring these men to task ? Was he sincere when he made that pledge, or did he expect then that the most of those enumerators would telegraph the reply that most of them did ? Why, Sir, these replies are on the face of them, absurd, as the member for Peel (Mr. Blain) pointed out. Fancy a commissioner having the hardihood to telegraph an hour or two after the receipt of the telegram by him that there were none of these circulars in the hands of his enumerators. I know there were some in the riding of East Simcoe, and when the officers wired that they did not know whether there were any there. I can prove that they were not in a position to know it. There must have been at least twenty-five enumerators iu that district, if not more, and it is not possible, much less reasonable, that these men could have been in a position to wire back as they did.
Now, the lion, minister made a pledge the other night, and that was that if he discovered any one of these men guilty of wrongdoing he would be punished and punished to the bitter end. On the strength of that statement the hon. minister felt that he was bound not to ask the House to vote money to pay men who have been breaking the j law and who have been perjuring themselves. Surely the hon. minister is not going to ask the people to give their hard-earned money, the money of this country, to men who are, to-day, in the most brazen way, admitting the fact that they have been perjuring themselves. It will not do for the hon. minister to say, that this circular was sent out without his authority, or to say that having discovered this illegal circular he has washed his hands clear of the whole tiling and that he is absolved. I trust the lion, minister will give another assurance to the committee that he proposes to set the criminal law in motion and endeavour to see what can be done, particularly in view of the statement he made, not a week ago, that this matter should be probed to the bottom and tihat if any persons were found guilty of j wrong-doing they would be punished. Does
the hon. minister propose to pay the enumerators who have been shown to be guilty of wrong-doing ?

I propose to pay the enumerators for the work [DOT]they have done.
'Mr. BLAIN. I would like to read this telegram from Algoma :
Fort William, 16th April. Sydney Fisher, Ottawa.
Have received schedules, hut did not give them to enumerators. No authority to do so.
This is a proof from the hon. minister's own official that he received these circulars but he had no authority to distribute them. Here is another telegram. I would like to ask the hon. minister if he has ascertained from E. A. Mortor, the commissioner for Algoma, who supplied him with these schedules.
No.

I would like to read this other telegram from the district of Fron-tenac :
Minister of Agriculture, Ottawa.
Enumerators have no schedule nor have I been asked to furnish one or allow them any such schedule. They are using schedule received from census office only. The schedule which you refer to is exclusively the business of the Frontenae Liberal executive.
Here is another from South Grey :
Durham, Ont., April 17th, 1901.
A. Blue.
No enumerator in my district has or had the political schedule. I got a bundle, hut never thought of using them; I am sure they were not supplied from any other source.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if he has taken any steps to find out who supplied that circular to these enumerators who were under the direct control of the minister.

I do not think it is in any way my duty to find out where this circular came from as a matter of the administration of my department. If my officers receive papers and make no use of them iu their official capacity I do not think it matters in the administration of my department. I do not propose to make an investiagtion as to where these circulars came from. The only information which I have, and which the hon. gentleman may have if he chooses to look it up, was given ill an article that I read in the Globe. It is sufficient because it seems to me to be an accurate statement and from other evidence (that has come to me in different forms I believe it to be a true statement of the facts.

The hon. gentleman says that he does not propose to make any further investigation as to the commissioners who | have received the circular and have made I no use of it. Would lie tell the committee what he proposes to do with those gentlemen

394S-
who have received it and who have made use of it ?
I have ordered them to immediately destroy it and not to give out any information they have obtained. I am informed that they have done so.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if the Prime Minister of the province of Ontario has corresponded with the hon. gentleman, or with the chief commissioner, in respect to this circular.
No.
The hon. gentleman is not aware whether the commissioner has received any communication or not ?
1 am perfectly satisfied with it.
Has the hon. minister that gentleman's authority for stating that ?
Yes.

Will the hon. minister be good enough to lay on the Table copies of the telegrams sent to these different enumerators who admitted that they had been using that circular, and the replies senr by them stating that they had destroyed the schedules that they had filled up ?

I have given the telegram which was sent. There was no other sent. I have also given the replies. These are all I have, except a letter or two which lias been received explanatory of the replies and which I shall be very glad to lay on the Table of the House.

What does the hon. minister think of those enumerators who may have used this circular that they got from some other source, not from his department ? They may have used it during the time they were taking the census, collated this information and given it out afterwards. Does he really think they have violated their duty, and their oath ?

[DOT]Certainly, if any census commissioner gets information while taking the census which he gives out afterwards he has violated his oath and his duty. I have no information that leads me to believe that any census enumerators have done that.
I thought, in the list that was given, the minister said there were some who had used it.

Some of them had this circular in their [DOT]possession and probably obtained some information, but they destroyed all these circulars immediately they were warned that they must not give out any information.

I understood the hon. minister to say a little while ago that in three counties, not that possibly they had used them but distinctly and emphatically, that they had used them. I now understand the hon. minister to suggest a qualification by saying that only possibly they had used them. It is important to know what position the hon. gentleman takes in regard to that.

If I did not use the words exactly I would like to say that now. My information was that these schedules were in the hands of some of the enumerators in these three counties. There was no statement that they actually used them, that they filled them up or used them in any way, although it would be implied that they had obtained some of that information.

I want to call the attention of the hon. minister to what I think would have been regarded as his duty in that particular. I quite apprehend that the hon. minister, having been driven from point to point, is disposed to take a desperate position. Whether he shall in the end maintain his position or not is not of so much importance to me as to state definitely what I conceive to be the duty of that hon. gentleman in that regard. We have, in the first place, the fact admitted by the hon. minister 'that he has one of these circulars in his possession. I do not assume that circulars come into the possession of a department by any means other than the ordinary channels of communication. This is not the time of the year when Santa Claus is distributing his favours, and I do not know whether the hon. minister proposes to have it go to the country that he does not know from what source that circular came. I know we have had more than one instance in which the ministry have been woefully ignorant of what has transpired in their departments. I do not know whether the minister wishes to have this added to the several instances in which responsible ministers have sought to escape responsibility on the plea that that they do not know what their department is doing.

So that the hon. gentleman will not go on the wrong track, I may say that I told an hon. gentleman a little while ago that I received the circular from one of the commissioners attached to the letter which he wrote me confirmatory of the telegram, in which he said that he had seen the circular. I cannot tell who it was.
We did not hear it across here. You must speak louder.
I am sorry the hon. gentleman was either out of the House or was inattentive.
None of us lieard it.

I am willing to take the minister's explanation, tout, although I listened with the greatest attention, not a single word of that statement came to my ears. I now ask the minister from whom the circular came ?
I cannot tell exactly which of the commissioners it was, tout I will look up the letter and lay it on the Table.

I presume the department is carried on in a business way, and that communications to it are promptly catalogued, so that the minister may be able to give us that information. I call the attention of the minister now to a matter of vital importance to the people of Canada. It is not disputed that in three counties these circulars have been in the hands of tlie census officers. We all know that officials entrusted with the administration of justice and the enforcement of the laws are watched with the greatest jealousy, and in order that the rights of the people should be secured, that is absolutely necessary. In the courts of justice, the slightest tampering with the most subordinate officer is punished in the most summary and exemplary way. Should any one attempt to suborn a witness or to approach a juryman, that person would be punished at once by the judge of the court. Does the Minister of Agriculture stand in a less responsible position in regard to these matters ? Does he wish it to be understood that having discovered that his officers had these papers in their possession, which to use in the slightest degree would cause them to violate their oaths, does he wish us to believe that he can discharge his full duty to the public when he comes to this House and says : It does not affect the administration of my department ; I wash my hands of the whole affair : it is of no concern to me. He tells us that on the night of the 15th of April it was his opinion that the guilty parties should be followed up and punished in the most exemplary manner, but. to-night he reconsiders the situation and tries to throw the blame on the shoulders of a political organization. He will now make no inquiries as to by whom these papers were sent to the enumerators. The minister says they did not come from his department. That may be, but they came from some source, and they were used in violation of the law. and I emphatically say that it is the duty of the minister to find out at least from what parties the enumerators obtained these documents. Nay. more. I submit for the consideration of all fair-thinking men. that when the law has been violated, when it has been sought to tamper with the oaths of public officers, it is the duty of that minister to institute an immediate and searching investigation, to discover who were the guilty parties. Can the minister even now
assure this House that these papers which have been found in the hands of the enumerators of at least three ridings, have not been actually filled up in violation of the instructions of the department and in violation of the law ?
All such documents have been destroyed according to the statements of the commissioners, and, therefore, the information never can be given out.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I understood the minister to say that having seen this statement in the Globe of the 19th, page 9, he was satisfied that that statement was published by Mr. Smith, the chief organizer of the Liberal party.
I thought it was signed by him.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
You most certainly led the House to believe that that was a statement made by the Liberal organizer. I find now that it is not on the editorial page, it is not in the correspondence column, it is not signed by Mr. Smith or anybody else, but. because it appears in the Globe the minister thinks it is all right. It is headed :
' For organization.-Alleged census circulars were distorted-Forms used to assist in assessment and at courts of revision-Nothing fraudulent or improper in their issue- A customary practice.' It goes on to give the side of the Liberal editor or some correspondent, who refused to sign his name, and it publishes what appears on the back of this document : ' Dominion of Canada, province of Ontario.' It goes on further and says :
Two copies to be prepared by the gentleman so chosen for each polling subdivision and sent to the Liberal candidate in the last provincial election or candidate now nominated for the next provincial election.
I defy any Liberal in this House to say that in each polling subdivision there ever has been a man named every year to go around and ascertain those who were over sixteen years and under twenty-one. It never has been done, and it is as clear as day that it was an attempt to get the census enumerators to do this political work. It says :
By the gentleman so chosen for each polling subdivision.
Who did that refer to ? It refers to the enumerator and no one else. But. because this statement is published on the back page of the Globe, without any signature, the minister tries to lead the House to believe that statement is made by a responsible officer of the Liberal party, when it is nothing of the kind. Yet, the minister has the hardihood to stand up and say : Although my officers have been caught redhanded. with these documents in their possession, and have used them, I am not going

to find out where they came from, whether they were printed by the commissioner in Ottawa or up in Toronto.
I take the whole responsibility of saying that they were not printed by the commissioner or any other officer of my department.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman himself says that this document was authorized by Mr. Smith, the organizer.
I said I thought it was signed by him.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: You said it was signed by him and came from him. I said it was editorial matter. You contradicted me. I said it was editorial by the reading of it, but was not In the editorial column, and was not signed by any one. It is simply an excuse, probably written by the census commissioner.
The hon. gentleman knows that such a statement is unworthy of him.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: No, I know the commissioner. The hon. gentleman wanted a political friend of his from Ontario who would do this dirty work for him, and have his officers gather up political information.
No.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
His officers have been doing it, and he refuses to give us a committee to trace this matter. We can call witnesses who can say where they got these papers, who sent them, and whether they were sent by Mr. Smith, the organizer, or by Air. Blue, the commissioner. We can find that out if the hon. gentleman will do liis duty and press the matter home. These circulars are in the hands of his officers, and we want to know liow they came there -who printed them and sent them there, and for whose benefit they were to be filled up. Wras it to help Air. Ross and his candidates in the next election ? That is what we want to find out. Why should we vote $250,000 to gather information to help Air. Ross and the Liberal party ?
The 31INISTER OF AGRICULTURE. AVe are not doing it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The documents are in the hands of your officers for that purpose.
They are not.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
How can the hon. gentleman say they are not when we have the statement from the commissioners that they are ? They probably did not go to the commissioners at all; they may have gone to the enumerators. not to the commissioners. These circulars may have been supplied to Mr. TAYLOR.
the local candidates or to some one else to be placed in the hands of the enumerators and the commissioners may have known nothing about them. Some of the commissioners admit that some of the enumerators used them; yet the minister refuses to give a committee. We on this side of the House will do our duty. AA'e will stay here until Christmas, if necessary, to have this matter investigated.
You have a good chance to stay till Christmas.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
AA'e can stay. The hon. gentleman says :	I know that a fraud has
been committed on my officers for the benefit of the Liberal party in Ontario, and yet I refuse to prosecute ; you may stay till Christmas if you like, but I will not give the information, nor prosecute these officers of mine who have been caught red-handed in violation of their obligation. This is the sort of gentleman we have running the affairs of this country. Then he states as a responsible minister that he is satisfied with the statement made in the Globe of the 19tli, page 9, by Air. Smith, the organizer of the Liberal party, when neither Air. Smith nor any one else dare sign that statement, because it is not in accordance with the facts.

I wish to point out to the minister and to the hon. member for Annapolis (Air. Wade), who seems to be so proud of this thing, that the very commissioners appointed by the minister speak, of these schedules in a way which of itself ought to cause the minister to do something. The telegrams which I am going to read are telegrams sent by these commissioners to the Alinister of Agriculture. Here is one from Air. AlcDougall in Aliddle-sex, which says :
Have only seen one bogus schedule.
Does the hon. member for Annapolis approve of bogus schedules being circulated in this country ?
AA'hy does the hon. gentleman refer to me ?
Because he interrupted the hon. member who was last speaking, and laughed at the matter.
I did not. I merely tried to attract the attention of the good-looking member in front of him, and failed to do so. I hope he does not object to our smiling. AA'e are not so ruffled as he thinks.

The hon. gentleman is not as accustomed to looking at good looking men as we are.
Some lion. AIEAIBERS. Hear, hear.

I want the minister and the hon. member for Annapolis to un-
