derstand that this sort of bluff will not make us sit down any quicker. The commissioners appointed by the Minister of Agriculture call these bogus schedules, and I want to ask the minister and those sitting behind him, particularly the hon. member for Annapolis, whether they want bogus schedules to be circulated through the province of Ontario to accomplish something that ought not to be accomplished according to the view of the commissioners.
Do you want me to reply 1

Yes. I do not understand what the hon. gentleman means. This is the telegram :
I have only seen one bogus schedule Saturday last, and ordered it destroyed as soon as seen. My enumerators have been warned by me to use only schedules supplied by me.
The commissioner is a better guardian of the public interest than the Minister of Agriculture, because he does go to the trouble of warning those below him to use only the schedules supplied by him. I think the Minister of Agriculture ought, in the interests of the country, to find out who sent that bogus schedule there, and how many more are in circulation.. Now, 1 will refer to another telegram signed D. J. Lynch, Campbellford :
Your telegram received. Have sent instructions to each enumerator to destroy circular if he has it in his possession.
Has the Minister of Agriculture any intention ol' following that up, and ascertaining how many of those circulars went to Campbellford, and whether Mr. Lynch's instructions have been carried out ?
Then, we find a telegram from Lynch saying he could find no such circulars in Woodstock, but was sending inquiries out of town to see if any were to be found there. The last part of the telegram is rather contradictory of the first, tie wires that he has not seen any of these documents in Woodstock, but at the same time he sent out of town to know if any could be found there, and to that he got no answer, xind that satisfies the hon. minister. I do not know whether the hon. minister called these documents bogus circulars or schedules in the telegrams he sent, and to which he has this answer, but I do know that the answers sent to the minister show that his own servants called it a bogus schedule, and although we have 'the evidence on the Table of the House that these bogus schedules are in circulation, apparently nothing is to be done about them. I do not see how the hon. minister is going to get out of it. What is he going to do ? He should at once use what means may be at his disposal to trace up the issue of this fraudulent or bogus schedule. Some one is guilty. It has been asserted here that this document had the words ' Dominion of Canada ' written on the back. Is a circular to go out, marked Dominion of Canada, and called bogus by the servants of the administration, a circular unauthorized, which is practically a forgery upon the officers of the department, and are no steps to be taken to find out who is the guilty party ? The Minister of Agriculture is satisfied that everything necessary has been done and that we ought also to be satisfied, but he cannot expect us to take that view of it. Although I am a young member, I am confident that 1 am not going out of my way when I say that if acts of this kind are allowed to go without investigation and unpunished, we will be creating a very mischievous precedent, and consequently the Minister of Agriculture will have to give us more satisfaction if he expects the item to pass.
I would like to ask the minister if D. F. Macdonald is a commissioner or one of the enumerators.
He is not a commissioner and I do not think he is an enumerator, but I cannot tell offhand.

This gentleman is a man of great literary ability, and the hon. gentleman's commissioner is quite well aware he is. He is a man quite competent to frame a circular of this description and formerly was part of the machine in Ontario. In order to prove his literary abilty and his competency to get up a circular of the description of the one under discussion, I will read a short article from his pen. He was formerly an Ontario official and belonged to the machine. He visited my county once, and this is what he said about the honest electors in my district in a letter he addressed to Mr. Aubrey White, deputy commissioner of Crown Lands for the province of Ontario :
Rodney, Jan 6th, 1899.
Dear Aubrey,-Here we are again, away from the rocks and charred pines of Nipissing and the nervous and excitable Frenchmen. Here's where there is hot work in store for us. Both candidates are popular, and lots of good workers on both sides. Here's where you can meet the sons and grandsons of the men that Argyle drove from their homes, the islands of Mull, Islay, Tiree and Ganna. As a class they are small in stature, dark and swarthy, with that greasy, fish-fed look that is found among the west coast fishermen. They are as tricky as pet foxes, and as sly as a tailor's pet monkey, and can lie as deftly as a Russian diplomat. They have pretensions of honour and pride from the teeth outwards. They are a slick, polished gang, in the majority. They are no more to be compared to the brawny and brainy men of old Glengarry than a mouth organ is to be compared to a Heintzman piano. We have one ward here with twenty-five Pattersons on the voters' list, twenty-three out of that are Tories. In the same ward or polling subdivision there are twenty-nine Campbells, fourteen of them are Tories. The McColls and MacDiarmids without number are Tories; the McCallums and McPhersons are solid Tories ; the Macdonalds, as usual, are divided. The McLartys, McVicars, McGregors and MePhails are Tory through to the spinal nerve. The McKays are Gritty, the Purcells are

395G
Liberals to a man, and the doubtful fish are the Swishers, Scheitzers, Schneckeubergers, Sehills, Schmidts, Krauses, Kruppes, Keillers, Leibners and the Ousterhaughs. When you get that German brood intermarried with the McPhees, McFaddens, McPhails and MeAulays, they make a queer brood of Scottish Canadians from a doubtful ancestry. They had a hot time at the nominations yesterday in Dutton. I was not there. They are going to have a big time here in Rodney to-night. They have 500 torches ready for the flames to meet G. W. Ross at the station this evening. The brass band will be there. The McRays, the McGugans, the Mc-Ivors, MeRorys and McRitchies will be there. The Garchies, Dugalds, Duncans and Donalds, with Alberts, Conrads, Carlos, Gottliebs and Jacobs will be jumbled up in a British mixture. Sauerkraut and porridge. Limburger cheese and salt herring. Bologna sausage and haggi3, lager and hot Scotch, lamb-scouse and brose, and the riding is any man's to-day. I am going to St. Thomas in the morning to meet Preston. We will win if we can. Keep our fellows fighting mad until Thursday night.
Hoping you are all well,
I am, as ever, yours,

Surely that is the production of a gentleman quite competent to get up this circular ; and if the Minister of Agriculture would jmake a close inquiry, he might find that Mr. Macdonald has something to do with this circular.
It's a pity the hon. gentleman read that description of his own county in the absence of the hon. member for West Elgin, who no doubt would have enjoyed it.
He has seen this and heard it read often enough.

No doubt the commissioner for Northumberland thought he was doing his duty when he sent that telegram. It is ail very well to laugh and make light of this thing, but it. is a serious matter. The hon. minister does not appreciate the position he is occupying when he says he does not care. For a minister of the Crown to say he does not care, when he knows from one of his officials that a fraud has been perpetrated, lie is taking a stand which does not at all reflect credit upon himself. I am sorry that lion, gentlemen around me feel like making sport of this. I do not think that this is a subject that we should make sport of. Here we have officials paid out of the Dominion exchequer to take the census, and the hon. gentleman knows deep in his heart, that there is a job there being-perpetrated by these men, because he has telegrams that inform him of it. Now he gets up to-night and waves it off by saying that he had telegrams from his officials and that they state that they know nothing of the matter. I would ask the hon. minister what chance these officials have to know the facts ? How can they know whether these documents are in the hands of the enumerators or not ? He sends out a telegram late at night and the next morning Mr. INGRAM.
at ten o'clock telegrams are sent to him by the commissioners stating that they have made inquiries.
Now, take the case of the riding that I have the honour to represent ; the commissioner lives at Campbellford. It is 30 miles, I suppose, to the village of Colborne in the front part of the riding in which I live. How could the commissioner know whether the documents were in the hands of the enumerators or not ? I know, and the people of the country know, that the enumerators had these bogus documents in their hands. He tells ns that he has instructed the commissioners to have them destroyed. How does he know that that has been done ? He bas a telegram from partisans through whose hands perhaps, bogus documents may have gone, though they may not-I would not say they had. But, knowing East Northumberland as I do, I know that if the enumerators had these documents in their hands the commissioner could not get them away so speedily. The hon. minister pays no more attention than if he were not responsible in this matter. He is looking around as though it were no concern of his. And he has the hardihood to tell us that he does not care. That is a most astounding statement. He does not care whether his enumerators in East Northumberland are perpetrating a job on the people I have the honour to represent or whether they are not. I would like to know if he did not feel responsibility enough to inquire into the facts, when he knows that these circulars were put into the hands of the enumerators of East Northumberland '! Does lie not feel it to be his duty to make inquiries what was done with the circulars ? Does he think that the mere assertion will lead me to believe that the commissioner can possibly know that the circulars have been destroyed, or that they had not been filled up and put into the hands of the Grit heelers in that riding ? I think that when he thinks this matter over seriously he will not treat it so lightly. Even if he does. I know that the people of this country will not treat it as lightly as he does. How can he say that he does not care when he knows that circulars have been put into the hands of his officials, and that they may have given information in violation oif their oath-and I am doubtful, if this was not done in the very riding that I have the honour to represent. I state earnestly and sincerely that the hon. minister is shirking his duty. That may not seem strong enough language, but it is the strongest that I can use without being offensive. I think the hon. minister is shirking his duty when he says that he will not trace this matter further than he has done by simply bringing out the telegram from the commissioner of East Northumberland to the effect that he is doing his duty. I think

this is too serious a matter to he let go in that way, and I hope the hon. gentleman will reconsider his action and take some steps to bring to justice those who have the circulars in their hands. He knows from the telegram or ietter he got from Bast Northumberland that these officials have these documents in their hands, and, perhaps if he made further inquiries he would learn that these bogus schedules have been filled up and are now in the bands of the Reform party of East Northumberland.
Are there letters in connection with the telegrams from the other two counties ?

Here is one signed by Charles Young, assistant census commissioner of Algoma, dated from Richard's Landing :
Since the receipt of your telegram, April 16, I made diligent personal inquiry among my enumerators regarding schedule entitled ' male residents sixteen years and over.' None of them know anything about it.
I am satisfied no such schedule has ever been put in the hands of my enumerators, at least in this part of division No. 44.

The hon. gentleman did not understand my question. He has produced a letter in confirmation of a telegram from one of the counties in which the circular has been used. I would like to know if he has letters from the other two counties in whicli they were used ?
I am not aware of any such letter. There is none on this file. I do not think there is one from North York.
Is that one of the counties in which it was used ?

Yes. Allow me to quote the telegram from North York :
Have received such document and am making every effort to have it stamped out.

There is a letter from North Hastings, as follows :
I was away when your telegram of the 17th inst. came to Marmora asking if I had seen or heard of alleged fraudulent schedule. I at once followed up the enumerators and found some of them had blank papers to fill in the names of males sixteen years and upwards. The enumerators never put a name on any of those papers. I took all those papers from them. I took the enumerators with me to the store and burned the papers in their presence. I am now going to Maynooth, fifteen miles from here, and will burn all the papers you speak of.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) WILLIAM KELLY.
I understand there is a telegram from North York, and that that is one of the counties in which this circular was found in the hands of the enumerators ?
Yes.
The hon. gentleman has made the statement that in each of these counties the circular has been destroyed. I would like him to state to the House how he knows that it has been destroyed in North York.
I am informed there is a letter from Mr. Elliott stating that they were destroyed.

It seems to me it is a matter of sincere regret that the Minister of Agriculture should have taken the position he has in this matter. The hon. gentleman's attitude to-night is entirely different to what it was on a former occasion. He was going to punish the offenders then. I ask the hon. gentleman if he expects, in face of his stubborn refusal to make any inquiry into this matter, that any reasonable man in Canada will believe that he does not know who issued these circulars, and know all about it. The parties who put that circular into the hands of his enumerators endeavoured to commit a high crime in that they endeavoured to induce these enumerators to commit perjury; yet the hon. gentleman, with a wave of the hand, declares that it is none of his business. I have no hesitation in saying that it is the duty of the minister and of the chief commissioner to see that his officers are not tampered with. I assume, of course, that there was no disposition on the part of the officers under his control to commit an act of that kind or to connive at it. But that does not absolve the hon. gentleman from [ his duty to make an inquiry and to see that

tlie guilty parties are brought to justice. On a former occasion the hon. gentleman made this promise :
I have stated, and I state again, that it anything has been done beyond the law and the requirements of the duty of the enumerators, *they will be brought to task, and it will be seen by me as head of the department under which they are working that they do their work legally, lawfully, properly, and according to the strict letter of the law which lays down their duty. If any of them do anything which is wrong, they will be brought to book and prevented from doing it in the future. As regards an investigation, I will find out the facts of the matter, and I will be guided by the facts that I discover in my departmental search and inquiry.
Now, it is a fair question to ask if tlie bon. gentleman lias made that investigation ? If be has, I think it is a reasonable conclusion that be is in possession of full information to know where that circular originated, and by what machinery it was placed in the hands of the enumerators. Why. one of the enumerators, listening to the telegram, declares that he had bundles of them. Now, if the hon. gentleman has failed to carry out his pledge to parliament that he would investigate, then he must take the responsibility. I ask him now if he will inquire from his commissioners, and if he will investigate as he promised, and endeavour to wipe off the blot on his administration ?

I agree with the hon. gentleman that there does not seem to be any mystery as to where these circulars came from. The statement in the Toronto Globe that I alluded to, I have uo doubt is perfectly correct. I daresay the commissioners who have received it, if they know where it came from, would not hesitate to say so. But it does not seem to me that it matters much, so far as taking the census is concerned, where that circular came from, so long as it is not made use of. I have taken the steps which were necessary to prevent them being made use of. I found by returns and statements of my commissioners that they have not been made use of by the officers'of the department, with the exception of two enumerators in their ridings, and in that case, I am informed they have been now destroyed. Therefore, so far as taking the census is concerned, these schedules have no further interest and have nothing further to do with the census. Under these circumstances, I cannot see that there is the slightest duty resting upon me to make any further investigation into the matter, and I decline to do so.
Mi'. BENNETT. Now we understand where the minister stands. The minister is prepared to brazen it out. Mr. Ross did not attempt to brazen it out in the local legislature, but he did attempt to treat the Mr. CCANCY.
matter lightly, and for so doing he received a sharp rebuke from the Montreal Witness. The "Witness pointed out that, on a thorough review of the circumstances, the facts were these. Here, were men appointed by this government taking a solemn oath that they Would perform the duties that were allotted to them, and among the duties allotted to them is not to ask any information outside of the schedules, not to convey any information that is given by the parties whom they interview to outside parties. The law goes far on this question. Hon. gentlemen know that there is on the statute-books of this country a law that meets this very case. It says :
Every officer, census commissioner, enumerator and other person employed in the execution of this Act, before entering on his duties, shall take and subscribe an oath binding him to the faithful and exact discharge of such duties.
Then it goes on :
Every officer, census commissioner, enumerator or other person employed in the execution of this Act, who makes wilful default in any matter required of him by this Act, or wilfully makes any false declaration touching any such matter, is guilty of a misdemeanour.
1 ask the hon. Minister of Agriculture if he does not hold that any man who, having taken that solemn oath that he will not divulge information, that he will not secure any information beyond that which is allotted to him or enjoined upon him by the instructions, goes outside of that oath altogether, as these enumerators admit they have done, should he punished. Is he not going to apply the law to them ? He cannot let the law stand still, because here is what the Act says in respect to that :
Every officer, census commissioner, enumerator or other person employed in the execution of this Act, who makes wilful default in any matter required of him by this Act, or wilfully makes any false declaration touching any such matter, is guilty of a misdemeanour.
The hon. minister asks ns to take this position : admitting that these men have been guilty, let any man prosecute them. It is not up to us to do that, but it is on the part of the hon. minister to do that, and more especially in view of the fact that the hon. minister made a solemn pledge here the other night that he would do that. Are we to take the hon. minister seriously ? Was he not acting honestly when he assured the House in these words :
I have stated, and I state again, that if anything has been done beyond the law and the requirements of the duties of the enumerators they will be brought to task, and it will be seen by me as head of the department under which they are working, that they do their work legally. lawfully and properly, according to the strict letter of the law which lays down their duties.
That was the pledge of the hon. minister the .other night. The minister felt his position keenly, the other members of tlie cabinet who were present felt that they could

not afford to treat tills matter as Mr. Ross had done. They felt that purnic opinion was against them. They had a lecture read to them from the Montreal Witness, and I am going to read it again to them :
If a government treats such affairs as this one as matters of no consequence, it is certainly losing its moral perception, and will soon forfeit the confidence of right-thinking people.
I would have supposed that there would have been some hon. gentleman behind them who would have risen with a reprimand, but they have all treated this matter in a most flippant manner. The hon. gentlemen behind the government seem to think this is an excellent joke, and they are prepared to vote this money to pay men who have been guilty of violating their oath. I want to point out that the census enumerators are paid by the day. if I understand rightly, and these men have been going round the country spending their time in procuring information which was not enjoined upon them by the instructions for the benefit of a political organization, as it is now conceded, and they are to be paid out of this vote before the committee. I am surprised that some hon. gentleman behind the government have not risen to demand that these men should be punished. I sympathize with the hon. Minister of Agriculture. He is in rather a bad box. He has been in a bad box in this census-taking business throughout. He had the work taken out of hi's hands in the province of Quebec. The hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Tarte) rode roughshod over him. The hon. Minister of Public Works appointed his tides Achates, Mr. Cote, to be assistant commissioner. In appointing Mr. C6t6 to be assistant commissioner, I think an excellent choice was made, because I think he is well qualified for the work. I admire his ability and cleverness, but the Minister of Agriculture was subjected to this indignity, and now the hon. Minister of Public Works is being subjected to another indignity at the hands of the ministers from Ontario. The other night, when he said he would carry out the criminal law, and promised that he was going to stand high in the estimation of the public, that he was going to deserve the respect of the Montreal Witness, that he was not going to be told that his moral perception was not good, he had to condescend to be lectured by the ministers from Ontario. They told him that he must not probe into this matter, because it was going to affect the Liberal organization in Ontario. So, the hon. minister has to eat the leek, which, I suppose, he has done first at the instance of the hon. Minister of Public Works, and next at the instance of these two ministers from the province of Ontario, who have forced him to take this position. I want to draw attention to another clause which has been pointed out to me :
Any document or paper, written or printed, purporting to be a form authorized for use in
the taking of the census, or to set forth gny instructions relative thereto, which is produced by any person employed in the execution of this Aot, as being such form, or as setting forth such instructions, shall be presumed to have been supplied by the proper authority to the person so producing the same, and shall be prima facie evidence of all instructions therein set forth.
Surely it is a subject of inquiry to find out who supplied these forms, but the hon. minister says he does not propose to interfere. He says that he is going to eat his words of the other night, when he promised to have the investigation. Section 20 of the Act says :
Whenever the Minister of Agriculture deems it convenient, he may, by special letter of instruction, direct any officer, census commissioner or other person employed in the execution of this Act to make inquiry under oath as to any matter connected with the taking of the census, or the ascertaining or correction of any supposed defect or inaccuracy therein.
The minister felt that he was not going to place himself in the position in which Mr. Ross had' placed himself in the province of Ontario, and in the position of being lectured as he had been lectured by the Montreal Witness. Now, we have another statement from the hon. minister, and his statement is, that there is to be no inquiry made, that the matter is to be treated in the most flippant manner possible. All I can say is, that if the minister proceeds in that way, I trust the great moral daily, the Montreal Witness, will say that he is an hon. gentleman who is losing his moral perception, and will soon forfeit the confidence of all right-thinking people. That is the position of the minister, and I repeat again that I think it is to be regretted that no member of the government deems it proper that this matter should be investigated and probed to the bottom.

The hon. member for East Simcoe and the hon. member for Both-well have both read quotations from the promise made by the hon. Minister of Agriculture the other evening. I have another quotation which I think a still stronger one than that read by either of these hon. gentlemen. It is in these words :
The hon. gentleman must have misinterpreted whait I said if he thought that I was desirous in any way of shielding anybody or of preventing the fullest investigation.
We are astounded to hear the minister say to-night:	I know not who put them in
their hands nor do I care. Surely that is not in accordance with his statement the other evening. These gentlemen opposite may find fault with us from Ontario for making such a fuss over this circular

Hear, hear.
Mr, INGRAM. The hon. gentleman from Cape Breton is quite a young member of this House and perhaps a little advice from one who has been here longer than he, will

lie of some profit to him. The colleague of this young gentleman is manly enough to stand up and say .what he has to say, but this young man has never attempted to my knowledge to occupy the attention of this House in the ordinary way. He seems to think lie will advance himself by continually interrupting, but I want to tell him it would be more in keeping with the dignity of the House if he would address the Chairman in a manly way, and I will be pleased to answer him if I can. If that young man pursues the course he started out with, lie will have his hands full before he gets through with this parliament.
Do not worry.

We in Ontario have been accustomed to this kind of conduct on the part of the Ontario government, and the oflieials of that government, but we will not allow the same thing to occur in this parliament Without protesting. Under the Ontario system the government ofticials think it their duty to do everything they can to influence the electors against the Conservative party, but we will not allow them if we can to interfere in Dominion matters. It is not sufficient for the minister to say that these circulars have been issued by the Liberal party of the province of Ontario. In justice to the Liberal party of Ontario X say that a large portion of the Liberal party in that province are honourable men and are as loud in their condemnation of this conduct as are the Conservatives. In justice to the honest Liberals of Ontario and to the honest Liberals of this Dominion, the Minister of Justice should hold an investigation to discover and punish the guilty parties in this dishonourable transaction. When these gentlemen opposite were in opposition 1 have listened to them night after night taking up much more of the time of parliament than we have, in condemning things less deserving of censure than this. For my part I believe that this committee should rise until the minister is prepared to announce that he is bound to investigate this matter and to prosecute the guilty parties.

The Minister of Agriculture gained the confidence of the country when he made his statement some time ago in regard to this matter. He elevated himself in the estimation of right thinking people, because they believed he was sincere in the promises he made. Some of his own friends said in my presence in Toronto that at least one member of his government was entitled to the respect of good citizens,-and 1 was pleased to believe he would carry his intentions out. I regret to find to-night that my confidence was misplaced. What has changed his mind ? He told us the other day that those who violated the law would be brought to task. They have not been brought to task, and why ? He admits that the replies to his telegram show Mr. INGRAM.
that these fraudulent circulars were in the hands of some enumerators. Inasmuch as these replies were sent on the same day as the telegram of the minister was received, it is clear that the commissioners could not have had an opportunity' of ascertaining from all tiie enumerators whether or not this bogus circular was in their possessions. The information they gave was probably correct so far as it goes, but it is quite clear that tiie circular could be in the hands of some of the enumerators without the commissioners knowing it. While the minister has discharged a portion of his duty, I regret to have to say he has not discharged his whole duty. It is incumbent on him to hold an investigation to ascertain' how many of these enumerators had the bogus circulars in their possession, where they got them from, whether they' have used them, and to what extent they had violated their obligations ns census enumerators. The minister has failed to carry out the promise he gave on a former occasion to do this. It is quite clear from all the evidence at hand that some one has imposed upon the enumerators and endeavoured to cause them to violate their oaths of office. Then it is the duty of the minister to discover who supplied the enumerators with these fraudulent circulars. Some person or persons must be guilty of that, and those persons should be punished. It is the duty of the minister to discover who those persons are and to punish them. So far as the minister had gone he has done his duty, but he should go further and he will neglect his duty if he does not go further. X want the attention of the minister to what I am saying, as I am endeavouring to speak respectfully in regard to this matter, which is one of vital importance to the people of this Dominion.
I think the minister should find out who gave these instructions, and X am sure the provisions of the law will enable him to reach them and punish them, which he should do If for no other reason than to prevent others from committing fraudulent acts in the future. We in Ontario have perhaps had greater reason to look with suspicion on this act than hon. members from the other provinces, because the people of Ontario have been repeatedly imposed upon and deceived. They have been counselled to violate the law, have practically been made to violate the law, and have not been punished, and when an effort has been made to punish them in the courts of the country, there has usually been a miscarriage of justice on the part of the justices of the peace appointed by the present Reform government of Ontario, or the parties whose duty it was above all others to enforce the provisions of the law. This is only another evidence that the fine Italian hand of the operators of the machine belonging to the Reform party has been made use of in this affair, and I regret that one of the officials
3965	APRIL 26, 1901	3966
from Ontario has been brought down here and put at the head of this department. I would be very sorry to fasten upon him the responsibility of it ; but knowing what the Ontario officials have done in the past, it is very difficult for us to believe that they may not in some way be connected with this transaction. D. F. McDonald's name has been mentioned to-night. I remember when a circular was sent to Algoma giving instructions two days before the election came on ; it was sent to a place where a great many men were employed, and D. F. McDonald forged it by changing the date, liis (fine Italian hand has been seen in many elections in the province of Ontario. Who took the Indians and squaws into a house and took the clothes off the Indians and put them on the squaws, so that they could vote, but D. F. McDonald ? The same man took the position of a deputy returning officer out of the hands of the man appointed to do the duty, and sat there all day in open violation of the law. Now we find the same kind of thing being done and in the same province. Who was it burned the ballots in the West Elgin election but one of the Ontario officials ? And when we find that one of these officials is brought down here and put at the head of this branch of the department, and this transaction shortly afterwards takes place, is it any wonder that we are a little suspicious, and that we ask that an effort should be made to find the guilty parties and punish them, whoever they are ? If that is not done, it will be evident that there is no desire to punish the guilty and have honest and truthful work done. That will be the opinion the people will hold of the hon. minister if he does no more than he has done up to the present time. I can only say I regret it exceedingly, because I have a very much better opinion of the Minister of Agriculture than his answers to-night would seem to justify, and I believe the country has a better opinion of him. After his statement the other night in this House, he established confidence between himself and the thinking people of the country, and they believed -that he would do his duty, and make an effort to find out who were the parties guilty of this rascality, and would give them the full benefit of the law. He cited those clauses of the Act providing the punishment for those who would do anything other than their duty, so that they would have in their minds what was in store for them. Does he attempt to carry out that promise ? I do not think he does, and until he does that, the people of this country will hold him responsible for being cognizant of wrong-doing and not attempting to find out who have failed to do their duty and who have attempted to make men perjure themselves.

speechtext:
The minister informed us a short time ago that he was satisfied, from an article that appeared in the Globe of the
19th, written by the chief organizer of the party, Mr. Smith, that this document was altogether prepared by the Liberal party. The article says it was sent to the parties for the purpose of getting information for making up the voters' lists. Now, let me read the replies from some of the hon. gentleman's officers-the commissioners, not the enumerators. The first is from Bradford :
April 17.-Have received such document. Am making every effort to have it stamped out.- Charles Elliott, Commissioner.
He had received the document, distributed it, and is now making every effort to have it stamped out. The next one is from my own county, from Brockville.
Took the steps indicated in your telegram re schedules yesterday before receipt of your wire.
The commissioner there, Mr. Macnamara, before he got the telegram, saw the announcement in the papers, and took the necessary steps himself, knowing what was going to happen. Here is one from Chesley :
I received the schedules you inquire about; have made no use of them.
Were these sent out simply for the purpose of making up the voters' list in the riding. Let me give another one :
Port Elgin, April 18.-Blank forms referred to reached me, but not one put into enumerators' hands or used in any way.
If these were for political purposes, why were they sent to all these commissioners ? Has the hon. minister inquired where they got them or whether there was a letter accompanying them ? I think the House is entitled to that information. Let me read some more. Here is one from Bolton :
April 16.-Some schedules the same as referred to in your message came to me by post some time ago. Did not come from your department. Did not distribute them among enumerators. Had instructions to do so. Schedules are still in my office, and have not been used.
Who gave those instructions ? Surely the House Is entitled to find out who was attempting to perpetrate this fraud. Has the minister inquired from this commissioner. Mr. Hutton, from whom he got this parcel and the instructions to distribute them ? Here is one from Belle River :
Re schedule, residents sixteen years of age and over, I have heard some were introduced, but have given instructions as by your telegram.
Here the commissioner again knew that they were to be used, and when he received that telegram, lie gave instructions to stop them. Here is a gentleman telegraphs to Mr. Blue from Durham that no enumerator in that district has or had this political schedule, but that he got a bundle but never used them, and was sure they were not supplied from any other source. What does that mean ? What other source were they not supplied from. It must mean that they were not supplied from any other source but the department.

The meaning is this, that they were not supplied in liis district to the enumerators, because he did not supply, them. The enumerators had not any of these circulars, because he did not supply them, and they did not get them from any other source.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
He says he got them, and it is the duty of the minister to find out from whom he got them. Here is another commisssioner, Mr. Kelly, from Marmora. He wires :
I will follow the enumerators immediately and destroy any of the papers alluded to in your telegram.
Evidently he got the papers and sent them out, and then set to work to destroy them. Mr. Blue telegraphed Mr. Kelly the following day :
Have you seen or heard of alleged fraudulent schedule in your district. Answer.
But we find no answer among the papers.
The hon. gentleman ignores the fact that I read a letter from Mr. Kelly in reply.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The letter is not on the file here. But, Mr. Blue asked for an answer by telegram, and to charge the cost of the telegram to the census commissioner. There is no telegram here.

There is a letter which I read.
Mr. TAYLOR, It ought to be on the file.
There is another file here.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The commissioner instructed Mr. Kelly to answer by wire, and to charge the cost to him. The presumption is that Mr. Kelly acted on his instructions, and did wire Mr. Blue, or else he ought to be dismissed. If he did not wire, but wrote a letter, he was not following his instructions. Then, we have a telegram from Mr. A. T. Macdonald, of Middlesex, saying :
Have seen only one bogus schedule, last Saturday and ordered it to be destroyed. My enumerators warned to use only schedules supplied by me.
He does not say where he got the bogus schedule. Then, there is a telegram from Peterborough, on April 16 :
I find on thorough investigation that the schedule mentioned has not been placed with any enumerator in my district. Neither myself nor any of the enumerators has seen such schedule.
The minister telegraphed on the night of the 15th, and on the 16th the commissioner, Mr. Robert Kerr, who has thirty or forty enumerators under his charge, wired back that neither himself nor any of his enumerators had seen the schedule. How could he

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: tell ? He had not time to find out. I have only gone through a portion of the file, but more than a dozen commissioners have told the minister that they received a bundle through the mails, and yet the minister says he will not find out where they came from. A crime has been perpetrated in sending these schedules to the commissioners for distribution to their enumerators, who are to get the information for the local legislature of Ontario, and thus violate l their oath of office, and yet the minister says he does not know where these schedules came from, nor does he care, and refuses to investigate. Evidently he knows, or has an idea who is responsible, and does not want the guilty party to be implicated. IVere these circulars sent postage paid, or were they franked from Ottawa ? We should get that information and the letter of instruction. One man says that he got the bundle and a letter of instructions, but he did not use them, and that they are lying in his office, but the minister refuses to do anything. The country, however, will expect the minister to act differently, and not attempt to shield the men who have perpetrated this fraud.

I rise again to protest against the conduct of the Minister of Agriculture. I do so on behalf of the Conservative party, and also of the honest Liberal party. Unless some satisfaction is given to the people, they will hold the minister responsible, and he will not hear the last of this for some time to come. It is easy for him to ascertain the names of those who gave these commissioners these circulars, and he is in duty bound to do so. I have no objection to honest warfare in political matters. I believe that the government is perfectly justifiable in appointing enumerators who act as chairmen, or take a prominent part in political matters, and, speaking of my own city, I have to say that in its fourteen division's the enumerators are largely chairmen of the Liberal committee meetings, and I believe they are too honourable to violate the oath they have taken, so long as they are performing their duties, by taking advantage of their position to furnish political information. It would be honest warfare if, for the purpose of supplying voters' lists or getting up registration lists, the Liberal party should get any information they can from these men who act as chairmen. The Conservative party would do the same thing were they in power, and what we do ourselves, I am generous enough to allow my opponents to do, but when the hon. gentleman will allow scoundrels-for it is only 'such who would attempt a warfare of this kind-to take an unfair advantage such as this, he is not doing his duty to his opponents in honest warfare or to his own friends, who are above conduct of this kind, or to the country. One of the commissioners in Elgin county is Mr. Moore. He had entire charge
39G9

of the last campaign in that electoral district. Mr. Moore is a perfectly honourable naan, so far as I know, and a good fair fighter in politics. But, so far as this is concerned, it is not within the usual line of fighting political battles, and it is taking an unfair advantage. Unless some action is taken by the minister, the statements that he has made will be made to ring on every platform in the province of Ontario, greatly to the advantage of the Conservative party, and to the disadvantage of his own friends. If that is what he wants, he is welcome to it ; but many quotations will be given of the statements made by him in this House, to show how the promise he made has been violated.

I do not admit that I have violated any promise ; on the contrary the promise I made has been carried out to the letter. The promise I made in substance was that I would investigate the state of affairs and would act in the matter if I thought it necessary. I have investigated the state of affairs through my officers ; and I find that, of 114 commissioners in the province of Ontario, 102 have replied that they know nothing about the circular, and have no trace of it in their division, nine say they have known of its existence, but no use has been made of it, and three who acknowledge that if has been in the hands of some enumerators, but state that they have taken steps to have the use of it stopped, and to have the schedules that were used destroyed. It seems to me very clear that whatever may have been the intention or the effort of somebody, there has been no material use of this schedule by the enumerators who were taking the census. A few, apparently, began to use it, but before any harm arose from their using it, the use of it was stopped and the instructions issued by me as head of the department have been carried out. I shall not give a legal opinion, but I wish to point out that the mere fact of this circular being in the hands of any individual is not illegal. If this was issued, as I believe it was, by a political organiaztlon in Ontario, the organizers had a right to send it out to members of their association. If it happened that commissioners or enumerators of the census were members of that organization, they had a right to have the circular. The wrong would begin only when the enumerators or commissioners began to use it in connection with the taking of the census. Apparently, some few commenced to do so. Their work was stopped. No harm to the taking of the census has in any way occurred, because there was no foundation for the belief that any of the information so acquired has been transmitted or made use of. Even if it was gathered, the results had been destroyed. Therefore, I cannot see or acknowledge that there is any 125
necessity for further investigation. The question as to who sent this circular does not seem to me to be material in the administration of the work and taking of the census.
Would the hon. minister say why not ?
Because I do not consider that it matters how it was sent out or who sent it. I take it that the people who sent it had a right to send it.' I am not quarrelling with their right to do so.
Hear, hear.

Yes, ' Hear, hear.' If a political organization chooses to send out circulars, as the organization of hon. gentlemen opposite have done over and over again, they have a right to do so. But, when the officers of the government begin to gather information for political purposes, I confess that they are doing wrong. And I have warned my officers to see to it that they do not continue it, and have warned them also that any information they may have gathered must be destroyed, and that has been done. That stop having been put to any wrongdoing in the matter, if there was any, it has prevented any evil arising from this matter in connection with the taking of the census. I do not see the need of any further investigation. As to who sent out this circular, I decline to be responsible, and I do not think it is my duty or the duty of my officers to inquire into the matter.

Surely, the hon. gentleman will see the distinction. The Liberal organization represents the Liberal party in the province of Ontario. Does he mean to say that the Liberal party in Ontario approves of this kind of thing 7
I do not know; I have not asked them.
In justice to members of the Liberal party who do not believe in this kind of thing, it is the duty of the hon. gentleman to find out who is responsible for it. It is his duty to his party.
I do not think so.

I think the hon. minister has laid down the most shocking doctrine I ever heard, when he says that no harm is done until such time as the enumerators have used these circulars. We have instance after instance in the Election Act, and in other Acts, where it is made a misdemeanour to tamper with or approach an officer or a voter. The hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that that is not a new feature, yet he declares that it will be .no harm for a man to perjure himself
I said nothing of the kind.
That was the effect of it- to perjure himself to send a man to the gallows, unless the man was actually hanged. The hon. minister has in so many words, justified that.
No.

I do not wish to misrepresent the hon. gentleman, but I think we had an unequivocal statement from him that he saw no wrong in men approaching his officials all over this Dominion, that the wrong would commence only when these men had begun to use these circulars. The hon. gentleman, by degrees, is becoming bolder
Hardened.

Well, I still have hopes of him. I shall not even now despair. The hon. gentleman has a pledge in this House, he has a pledge in heaven, that he will take steps to prevent officials from violating their duty. The hon. gentleman says he has carried out that pledge, that he has made an investigation. He sent out a warning to his officials, hastily, having been driven to do so, I am bound to say,"by the well-directed criticism that such a case deserves. But I challenge him to say that he has endeavoured to make any investigation. What he did was merely what must precede an investigation. I ask him if he has made further investigation than sending out these circulars to his own officials ?
Mr. Chairman
I wish to get an answer if the hon. member for West Huron will permit me. Has the hon. minister made any other investigation than to send out these instructions to his officials ?
I have told the hon. gentleman what I have done.

If the hon. gentleman will come down enough to tell this committee again-because I confess my dullness, and it seems to me that I have not had a straight answer from the hon. gentleman. Now, I ask the Minister of Agriculture if he has made any further investigation other than to send out those telegrams to his officials warning them not to use those circulars ?
That is what I have done.
Has the hon. gentleman done anything more ?
No.
Supposing the enumerators were still to go on and get this information, what position would the minister take ?
Did the enumerators get instructions to procure information for the department only ?
Certainly.

Now, the minister states that he is prepared to dismiss those officers who will not carry out the instructions, he also says they had received instructions, yet we have the acknowledgment from him this evening that there were at least nine or ten commissioners who did send out to get this information. Under the circumstances, I think those commissioners, at any rate, should be punished according to the hon. gentleman's promise.
If they do not comply with this order.

I fancy that our friends on the other side realize that to some extent they are beating the wind on this question. Hon. gentlemen from Ontario know perfectly well that it is the custom to send out circulars, of a somewhat similar nature to these, every year in order to instruct local parties to look after the revision of the voters' list, both in the spring and in the fall. Both the Liberal and Conservative parties are accustomed to send out circulars asking for information of this or a similar nature. Now, the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) was frank enough to admit the whole crux of the situatiou. He knows perfectly well, as other hon. gentlemen do, that a great many of the enumerators happen to be chairmen of the lulling subdivisions. In my own riding I know that some of the enumerators are chairmen of the polling subdivisions. In the past it has been the custom to send out circulars of that kind, either to the Liberal representative or to the chairmen of the various polling subdivisions. It happens this year that those circulars were sent out, as in previous years, to the chairmen of the polling subdivisions, and these happen to be in most cases the enumerators. I venture to say that if the truth were known it

would be found out that these circulars had gone only into the hands of those who are chairmen of polling subdivisions, and that those census enumerators who do not happen to occupy that position have not seen these circulars unless they have been shown to them by somebody into whose hands they have fallen. I think that is the explanation of the whole situation. I am satisfied that the hon. gentlemen opposite would admit that that Is the case. The article in the Globe from which the hon. member for Leeds and Grenville (Mr. Taylor) quoted, practically admits the origin of these circulars, that they were sent out by the Liberal organization.
Does the hon. gentleman agree with the minister that they are fraudulent-because the minister calls them fraudulent in his telegram ?

Never mind whether they are fraudulent or not. The member for Leeds and Grenville quoted from the Globe an article practically acknowledging that the circular sent out for this information came from the local Liberal organization. Judging from the uneasiness of hon. gentlemen opposite, it looks as if they anticipated defeat in the forthcoming elections in the province of Ontario. Now, Mr. Chairman, I am sorry to say that it has remained for a member of this House to impugn the honour and integrity of the gentleman who has been brought down here from Ontario as chief census commissioner, whose thorough uprightness has never yet been called in question. It is exceedingly regrettable that an hon. gentleman opposite should have coupled this gentleman's name with what he pleased to call the workers in connection with the machine.
Does the hon. gentleman refer to me ?
I refer to the hon. member for East Grey.

Then allow me to say that my words were, that I would be sorry to believe that he was connected with it, but the strange coincidence of these things happening so often amongst the officials coming down here from the local government, that it was enough at least to create suspicion.

The hon. gentleman's explanation only confirms what I am saying. He admits that he impugned the honour and integrity of the census commissioner, and that he did so without the slightest particle of foundation. I think this discussion should have been carried on without the display of feeling and warmth that have been manifested. While our hon. friends opposite are so anxious to know where the Minister of Agriculture got a copy of this circular, perhaps it would not be improper to inquire where the leader of the opposition got his copy, or where the member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) got his copy. As I remarked already, I think that hon. gentlemen opposite have been beating the wind without accomplishing very much.
The hon. gentleman has done me the honour of saying that I made an honest statement. I am sorry to say that I cannot return the compliment.
I consider where it comes from.
And where it goes to. I do not wish to be offensive to the hon. gentleman.
You were, nevertheless.

I do not wish to be offensive to him now. I agree with the hon. gentleman that both parties have sent out circulars. That has been done, but the inconsistency of the hon. gentleman's statement is this : he has forgotten the contents of this circular or he never would have compared it with the circular sent out by both of the political parties in the past. Does the hon. gentleman ever remember of a circular of this character being sent to enumerators ?
Take it as read; I know what it is.

I will read it again. The endorsement is as follows :
Dominion of Canada, Province of Ontario.
I never knew of a circular being issued by the Liberals of the province of Ontario under the heading of ' Dominion of Canada.' Then it goes on :
Month of	1901.
Male Residents,
Sixteen years of age or over.
Our circulars always read something like this : If they knew of any young men of the age of 21, entitled to vote, or about to be entitled to vote, to poreure their names in order to have them placed on the voters' lists. It goes on :
Polling Subdivision No	
Municipality of	
Electoral District of	
Per	
P. O	
To	
P. 0	
Two copies to be prepared by the gentleman so chosen for each subdivision and sent to the Liberal candidate in the last provincial election, or candidate now nominated for the next provincial election.
I never knew of a circular of that kind being sent out before.

Politics.
Date of Birth.
Month, Day, Year.
No. of Lot or House. Concession or street.
Post Office Address.
Nationality.
Religious Denominations and Church.
Remarks.
I never heard of a circular of that kind being issued before, and I am sure the hon. gentleman has never heard of any such circular. It was never intended that such a circular should be sent to the census enumerators. The circulars to which I refer were sent to a representative person in a constituency and he circulated them amongst those who were appointed as chairman. I believe this has been the practice of both political parties. What we complain of is that these circulars have been placed in the hands of the enumerators. That is striking below the belt ; it is not fair warfare. The Liberal party would be perfectly justified in using these enumerators if they isaw fit later on for the purpose of completing the voters' lists. That is fair warfare but it is not fair to make use of the enumerators while they are acting as such.
What evidence has the hon. gentleman that these circulars were placed in the hands of the enumerators ?
The telegrams state that.

Would the
hon. gentleman say what the telegrams state ? I was not in when they were read. I understand to the contrary.
Some other hon. gentlemen have read them ; I have not.
These telegrams have been read. They were read by the hon. member for East Simcoe, and there was nothing in a single telegram that was read that said they ever reached the enumerators.
Does not the letter of the minister show that they reached the enumerators ?

What I wish to say in respect to the anticipated defeat of the friends of hon. gentlemen opposite in Ontario, is that they are using this as a means to avoid that defeat. Fortunately, I think, the handwriting is on the wall.

Before the item passes, I think we ought to extend our sympathy to the Minister of Agriculture. I am sure that the hon. minister really wanted to do what was right in this case, and I have no doubt it is humiliating to the minister, now, looking back on his pledge and on his statement that it was his wish to have this matter probed to the bottom, to find that he has been overborne and that his wishes have been thrust down. I am reminded of the obituary of an ancient maiden lady which Mr. INGRAM
read that she meant well, tried a lot and failed much.

The press of the country have been instructing people, some of whom have been brought before the courts, that they are obliged to give this information, and have been assuring the people that they may give it witli the utmost confidence, because it will never be divulged. By the use of this circular it must be divulged.
We have prevented it being divulged.
The minister has given us the information that some of the enumerators had this information and that their schedules were burned.
They did not use it.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Wade) is giving information about a matter of which be knows nothing himself.
All I say is that there is no information before the committee that a single enumerator had used one of these circulars.

We are told that these circulars were in their possession and that they got instructions to burn them afterwards, but, does that show that they did not use the information ? I do not think it does. We are, on the one hand, instructing the people that when the enumerator acquires information he does not fulfil all his duties unless he keeps it secret, that he is not to ask for improper information and that when he gets that information he is not to give it out. Then, I ask : Will the confidence of the people not be shaken after knowing what has been brought out in connection with these circulars ? In view of what has been brought out in the House of Commons, would the people not be justified in not giving information because they have no guarantee of secrecy ? It will not be a very good course to take to bring them before the court and punish them for a refusal to give information when it goes out that the hon. Minister of Agriculture has refused to punish those parties who have abused their positions and who have successfully endeavoured to deceive and impose upon the people, by getting information from them that they should not get.
I notice, in a telegram from Cardwell, that Mr. Hutton says that he has the documents in his office now.

I would like to ask what foundation there is for this charge against the hon. Minister of Agriculture ? Hon. gentlemen opposite know as well as I do that the gentleman who happens to be the commissioner there is secretary of the Liberal Association. There has been nothing hidden, so far as I understand this matter. It seems that the provincial organization sent out blanks
What Liberal organization does the hon. gentleman refer to ?

For the province of Ontario. I do not see that there is any person trying to do anything secret or hidden in anything that has been done. I will refer to this particular case to show how foundationless the whole charge is. This gentleman, Mr. Hutton, happens to be the secretary of the Liberal Association. Some time before he was appointed commissioner he received the forms for the revision of the lists the same as the Conservative secretaries do. There is, nothing to hide about it.
It was the form of the circular I referred to.
Well. I have seen the Conservative circulars and I do not see any particular difference between them.
The hon. gentleman does not pretend to condone this.
Condone what ?
The offence against public morals.

What offence ?
Mr. CLANCY'. Do I take it that the hon. gentleman says it is no offence to approach the officers who are sworn to take the census ?

You have no right to take anything of the kind, because I was not going to condone anything of the sort, and no person who understands the matter would do so. I was about to point out how honestly this gentleman had acted in the matter. As an official of the Liberal Association he received the usual packages of blanks, and .what did he do? Did he issue one of these blanks to the enumerators ? Not at all. If he had done so there would be reason to find fault with him.

I am glad to hear the hon. gentleman say that he does not think this an offence, and he does not condone it. I conmmend that to the Minister of Agriculture, who thinks that no offence has been committed.

I ask the hon. gentleman to show me any one particular instance where any one committed an offence. My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) happened to know about Cardwell. I think he, as an hon. member of this House, ought to say that so far as that case is concerned, that this gentleman in his official position received these blanks, and instead of violating his office by giving them to enumerators, he is able to say that he did not do so.
But they have been used in other cases.

I am speaking of this particular case. The minister stated that 102 commissioners reported that they had not even seen these blanks. I think I will be borne out in the statement that blanks of a similar kind have been sent to officers of the Conservative Association.
What nonsense !
There is no nonsense about it. You have seen them, and I have seen them.
Not this kind.

There might be some little difference, but their forms are practically the same. It is only carping to draw the distinction. For many years the Liberal Association of Ontario has been sending out the usual blanks for the revision lists.
To Dominion officials ?

There is no evidence that any person connected with the Census Department from the minister down, had any knowledge, directly or indirectly, of anything of the kind. There is no evidence that any officer of the Liberal Association attempted to put these blanks in the hands of a census official.

The hon. gentleman from North Oxford (Hon. Mr. Sutherland), who is always fair in this House, wants to have light on the matter. It is admitted on all hands that at least a few of the enumerators did receive these circulars, although it is alleged that they did not use them. The hon. gentleman, (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) tells us it is wrong that any person whatsoever should endeavour to approach the census officers in this way. So far as the evidence goes, there is nothing to show that the census officials have evinced a disposition to do wrong, but the question is that some one did approach these enumerators, and those persons should be punished. It is the duty of the Minister of Agriculture to see to that.

The Minister of Agriculture took the most active and energetic measures within his power to take. The moment this was brought to his notice he took steps to see that the enumerators should have nothing to do with it. I merely wish to point out to the House that instead of the secretary of the Liberal Association receiving blame, he is, on the contrary, entitled to praise because he realized his duty to the full extent and he did not attempt to use these circulars in any way whatever. There was no authority on the part of the organizers, or upon the association in any way to ask any one of the census officials to use his office improperly, or contrary to the oath he had taken.
How innocent.

If the hon. gentleman wants to be fair, he knows that the evidence all shows what I have pointed out. My hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) tried, by twisting two or three telegrams, to show that the commissioners had been acting improperly, and had placed some of these circulars in the hands of some of the enumerators ; but, what did they do? They had them all withdrawn before they were used, and we find that in 102 cases they were never seen or heard of. This shows that the census enumerators were not used for this purpose.

This question has been pretty thoroughly threshed out, and the hon. gentleman who has just spoken has evidently not heard the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture, or he would not make the statement he does. He says that in 102 cases the commissioners heard nothing about the circular. Seven heard about it, got copies of it, and did not use them.
They got them as officials of the organization, not as census enumerators.

In three cases they acted upon them, but, in these three cases, on receiving the telegram of the Minister of Agriculture, they determined to destroy them, and all the information taken under them was burned. The fact remains -it is admitted by the Minister of Agriculture-that these circulars were sent out, and in three cases were distributed among the enumerators and acted upon ; that in seven cases they were received and not acted upon, and in 102 cases the commissioners had not heard of them.
I think my hon. friend will admit that if there were only three cases in the province of Ontario, it was not such a great conspiracy to do anything wrong.

The commissioners may have found it impossible to ascertain whether the enumerators had these circulars or not. These parties may have made use of the enumerators, and dealt directly with them. We are not blaming the government or the Minister of Agriculture for anything of that kind. The minister says that the first time he heard anything about the circular was when he saw it mentioned in the paper, and on the same evening that it was brought to his attention, he took every means possible to put an end to it. But, what we are insisting on is, that those persons who have violated the law and their oath shall not escape, but shall receive the punishment they ought to receive. If the Minister of Agriculture had promised in the first instance that some punishment would be imposed upon the parties who acted illegally and contrary to their oath, there would have been an end to the discussion long ago.
Did I understand the hon. member to say that he would lay the letters on the Table of the House ?
Yes-carried.

I do not think it is carried just yet, because we have not had the information which we are entitled to. The minister made the statement that 102 knew nothing about such documents, that nine heard of them, and that three had used them. But the telegrams read by various members of the House do not bear out that statement, but directly contradict it; they 'show that there was a very much larger number. The hon. member for North Oxford (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) says these schedules are not! fraudulent, that they are the regular official document of the party of which he is one of the leaders, if not the leader iu the province of Ontario. If that be the case, these men might say that they know nothing of any fraudulent document, as these are not fraudulent in that sense. Now, I say that these documents are not such as would be required for the purpose of revising the lists before the court of revision this year. I challenge the hon. member for North Oxford to produce last year's circular, and show that it was similar in substance to the document to which we have reference.
Send me over one of yours, and I will show you that there is very little difference.
I certainly have not one of ours under my hand.
Well, we will have one of them to-morrow, and will compare them.

I cannot remember having seen such a document in the Conservative party for years. We revise our lists in West York, and do not need any reminder of our duty in that regard. I do not know of any such letter having been sent out by the Conservative party for several years, or for any year, and the minister asks me to send him a circular which, so far as I know, has no existence whatever. The statement made in the Toronto Globe as to this document purported to give the backing on it, but did not give the document itself. It merely says that ' the following is the title on the back of the form which the opposition object to.' We object to more than that; we object to what is inside. We object to the census enumerators being furnished with this document. It. is perfectly clear that it was not intended for the purpose stated-for the revision of the lists, which occurs in May. Why did they ask for the religion or the names of those of sixteen years of age and over ? That could not be for the revision of the lists in 1901, because those of sixteen years of age and over have no right to be put on the list for

four or five years longer. It is only a false pretense to say that it was required for the revision of the lists in 1901. It was for the purpose of having a complete record for party purposes, for use in the future ; and it would fit in admirably with the next Dominion election. The boy of sixteen or thereabouts will be entitled to be a voter about the time when the next Dominion election comes around, if this House lasts its full term, and they wanted the enumerators to furnish a full statement for the information of their own political party at the expense of the people of Canada, which they had no right to do.
The Minister of Agriculture told us that prosecution would follow any violation of the oath of those enumerators. And then he tells us to-night that he is not going to make any further inquiry into this matter. Why has he violated the promise he made the other night ? Is it because the hon. member for North Oxford has told us that these bogus documents were regular business documents and that the government accept the responsibility themselves, in which case of coui'se they could not prosecute the hon. member for North Oxford and those other members who are responsible. The hon. member did not say that he fathered this thing individually, but that the Liberal party took the responsibility. Well, the Liberal party are the same identical individuals who fight the battles for the local legislature and the Dominion, and those two parties-the gentlemen in the House here and those who control the government of Ontario-are both responsible for this document, for its circulation, and for this attempt to get the enumerators to violate their oath to observe secrecy. In this case we find that the government are in the position of being the parties themselves whom they would have to arrest and prosecute. I can therefore realize the difficult position in which the Minister of Agriculture has put himself by promising to punish the perpetrators and then saying he does not care who they are and is not going to prosecute.

There seems to be a conflict between the Minister of Agriculture and the acting Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Sutherland). The latter made the challenge that no one could show that any of these circulars had been used by the enumerators, and the Minister of Agriculture made the statement that in three cases they had been used by the enumerators. Which statement is correct.
The hon. gentleman read a telegram, and I gave an explanation which I am sure he accepts as satisfactory.

Just one word about the telegram to the commissioner in Cardwell. He says :
Some schedules, same as referred to in your message, came to me by post some time ago. Did not come from your department. Did not distribute them among enumerators; had instructions to do so. Schedules are still in my office; shall not be used.
The acting Postmaster General says these were the customary circulars to send out ;tnd they were just sent in the ordinary way. Does that telegram look as if they were the ordinary circulars ? Yet this gentleman says he received them and had instructions to* send them to the enumerators. Furthermore, this gentleman still lias these documents, although the hon. Minister has promised that all such documents will be destroyed. Why have these not been destroyed ? This one telegram is sufficient proof that these circulars are now in existence, in the possession of a paid official of the government. What does the Minister of Agriculture propose to do with them ? The House must understand that the work is not all done and they may yet be used in that county.
